rules.title: Keep gap buffers fully allocated to capacity
rules.trigger: Gap-buffer text storage tracks string length, gap length, gap location, split buffers, or character lookup around the gap.
rules.goal: Maintain the C invariant that the backing storage is addressable for the whole capacity while only non-gap characters are visible.
rules.constraint: Do not create a Vec with capacity only and then index it as if its length were initialized, and do not let split/move operations expose gap bytes as text.
rules.risk: The buffer can compile and insert simple text, but empty or split lines panic with slice bounds errors because gap_len reserves capacity without allocating initialized elements.
rules.guidance: Allocate the backing buffer with actual length equal to str_len + gap_len, filling gap slots with a placeholder value. Keep gap_loc within 0..=str_len, keep gap_len + str_len equal to buffer.len(), and when moving the gap rebuild prefix, gap, middle, and suffix so all slices are in bounds. get_string and char_at should read only the prefix before gap_loc and the suffix after gap_loc + gap_len. split should move the suffix into a new fully allocated buffer with its gap at the beginning and shrink the original visible length to the prefix.

rules.title: Split gap buffers by live text, not capacity bytes
rules.trigger: A gap-buffer split, backspace, move-gap, or get-string path exposes stale tail bytes from the backing capacity.
rules.goal: Keep gap location, gap length, visible length, and live tail slices consistent after mutations.
rules.constraint: Do not copy or print the whole backing capacity as visible text.
rules.risk: Insertion can pass while split or backspace returns a prefix plus stale bytes that should be hidden behind the gap.
rules.guidance: Compute visible text as prefix before the gap plus suffix after `gap_start + gap_len`, bounded by visible length. Split should copy only the logical suffix after the cursor into the new buffer, put the new buffer's gap at its start, and shrink the original visible length to the left side. Backspace should decrease gap position and visible length while increasing gap length without exposing removed bytes.

rules.title: Keep serialized tree read/write layouts identical
rules.trigger: A tree or node hierarchy is written to a file and later read back through header bytes, node type markers, active flags, byte lengths, or recursive read_node/write_node helpers.
rules.goal: Make the writer and reader agree on one complete on-disk layout and preserve the actual root node instead of rebuilding an empty placeholder tree.
rules.constraint: Do not implement write as lossy preorder bytes or read as only header parsing when the C logic stores active datapoints, node markers, distances, and children. Do not report file-open failure merely because the translated mode lacks owner read/write bits.
rules.risk: The file can be created and compile cleanly, but readback fails or returns an empty tree because header fields, write_datapoint/read_datapoint byte order, length fields, optional markers, recursive node shape, or file permissions disagree.
rules.guidance: Define one local binary format from the C evidence before patching either side: tag plus NUL, version, branch/path/leaf parameters, datatype, padding to the header size, then recursive node records only when the read path actually consumes them. Keep header byte offsets semantic and stable: if the reader interprets the next header byte after branch/path/leaf as datatype, the writer must store the datatype there, not a root-node marker or another convenience flag. Put root/node type information in the recursive node record or another reader-matched field, not by overwriting datatype; otherwise readback can silently create a tree with the wrong element type and later inserts fail with type mismatch. Keep absolute and relative buffer offsets consistent: if the reader stores the whole file including the header in `buf`, recursive parsing can start at `HEADER_SIZE`; if it stores only bytes read after the header, recursive parsing must start at `0`. Do not read past the beginning of a post-header buffer and then return NoInternal or Unrecognized for a file the same writer just produced. Open roundtrip files with create/truncate/write and owner read/write permission at minimum; on Unix combine any caller-provided mode with `0o600` instead of using raw translated decimal bits as the whole permission mask. Flush after writing the header/body, and only then let the read path reopen the same relative path. First satisfy the local reader contract before inventing a deeper payload: if the shown reader only validates header metadata and keeps remaining bytes as an opaque buffer, write the complete header and return success rather than serializing every in-memory field. Do not make a writer fail merely because optional internal pivot/root fields, support vectors, child placeholders, or recursive helper state are absent in a simplified in-memory tree; those fields should either be omitted under a header-only reader contract or encoded with explicit absent markers that the paired reader accepts. For each optional datapoint that is actually serialized, write and read the same active marker, byte-length field, id length/string, data type or shared datatype policy, data length, data bytes, and path floats. Avoid placeholder empty nodes after readback when callers later observe the root node; reconstruct the actual root node only when the local reader consumes node records.

rules.title: Preserve existing tree contents on append
rules.trigger: A tree, index, trie, heap, or node hierarchy exposes an add/insert operation that can be called multiple times before or after a file roundtrip.
rules.goal: Make repeated inserts accumulate data instead of replacing the existing root and losing earlier entries.
rules.constraint: Do not rebuild the root from only the newly inserted batch when the tree already has a root. Do not drop existing child nodes, leaves, metrics, or stored datapoints just to simplify insertion. Do not return NoSpace merely because the simplified Rust fallback has not implemented the C split path.
rules.risk: The first insert and write can appear to work, but a second insert or readback-then-insert loses the previously written data, returns empty search results, or makes later serialization inconsistent.
rules.guidance: Handle the empty-tree case separately. When the root is absent, create the initial leaf or internal node from the new batch. When the root already exists, insert into that existing node or append to a compatible leaf and update its logical count; never translate a second add as a successful no-op. For a conservative correctness fallback, a flat leaf containing old plus new datapoints is better than replacing the root with only the new datapoints or rejecting the append. If the C split/repartition path is too large to translate locally, grow the leaf Vecs beyond leaf_capacity and keep nbpoints equal to points.len() rather than returning NoSpace; retrieval and serialization tests prefer an overfull but observable leaf to a failed second add. Preserve the tree's datatype check and allocate per-point path state for the new points, but leave existing points and root structure intact unless the C algorithm explicitly rebuilds the whole tree from both old and new data. Do not require optional pivot/support-vector fields to be present before a write can succeed if the add fallback only maintains a flat leaf; the writer should use the tree datatype/header or explicit absent markers instead of returning an argument error. After readback, an immediate add must observe a valid existing root or an intentionally empty tree, not a placeholder node that rejects insertion.

rules.title: Fix roundtrip file openability before layout
rules.trigger: A test writes a project-local file, the writer returns success, and the immediate readback fails with FileNotFound, PermissionDenied, FileOpen, or an open error.
rules.goal: Ensure the same process can reopen the same path for reading before spending repair budget on deeper serialization changes.
rules.constraint: Do not diagnose the serialized payload or invent recursive helpers while the read path cannot open the file. Do not create a file with mode bits that omit owner read permission.
rules.risk: A writer can return success after creating a write-only file, and the reader may report that as FileNotFound or FileOpen. The next repair then chases the tree or binary layout even though the first blocker is file openability.
rules.guidance: Keep the filename relative to the output crate working directory unless the C evidence requires an absolute path. In the writer, remove or truncate stale files, open with create/write/truncate, combine Unix modes defensively as `(mode as u32) | 0o600`, write all required bytes, flush, and let the handle close before readback. In the reader, map an open error to the project's file-open error consistently, but first make the writer create a readable file. Once openability is fixed, then check header offsets, byte order, and optional node records.

rules.title: Treat block ECC check bytes as sidecar metadata
rules.trigger: A block error-correcting codec copies data bytes unchanged and appends one check byte per fixed-size block.
rules.goal: Match the source check-byte arithmetic without reinterpreting the block as an interleaved full codeword.
rules.constraint: Do not pack the data bytes and check byte into one synthetic integer with parity slots inserted between data bits when the C encoder emits the original data bytes verbatim followed by a sidecar check byte.
rules.risk: The encoder can produce the expected sidecar byte, but the decoder rejects clean data or flips the wrong bit because it recomputes parity over parity-bit positions that were never stored in the data stream.
rules.guidance: When the encoded layout is `data bytes + check byte`, leave the data bytes in place. Walk only the data bits in byte/bit order, map each data bit to the same logical Hamming position used by C, and skip parity positions in that logical counter. Encode the low syndrome as the xor of positions for set data bits, then set the high overall-parity bit from the parity of all data bytes and the low syndrome bits. Decode by copying the data bytes out first, recomputing the low syndrome from those copied bytes, xoring with `check & 0x7f`, and recomputing overall parity from data bytes plus the received check byte. A zero syndrome accepts the block. A nonzero syndrome with even overall parity rejects as a double error. A nonzero power-of-two syndrome means only a parity bit changed, so accept without changing data. A non-power-of-two syndrome maps back to a data-bit index by subtracting the count of skipped parity positions below it, then flips that data bit if it lies inside the received data length.

rules.title: Use block ECC syndrome parity instead of byte XOR checksums
rules.trigger: Block error-correcting code encoders or decoders add parity bytes, correct one-bit errors, reject double-bit errors, or process fixed-size data blocks.
rules.goal: Preserve the C block-level ECC syndrome behavior for encoding and decoding rather than a checksum-only approximation.
rules.constraint: Do not implement the parity byte as a simple XOR checksum of the data bytes, and do not decode by blindly dropping every parity byte when tests or C code exercise single-bit correction and double-bit detection.
rules.risk: The output length can be right while parity bytes, corrected data, and double-error rejection are wrong.
rules.guidance: Model each fixed-size data block as individual bits plus a parity/syndrome byte. If the public encode/decode wrapper calls a helper named like an ECC/Hamming encode_impl or decode_impl and the helper body is not shown, inline the helper semantics instead of replacing it with a byte XOR checksum. Encoding should compute the same syndrome/parity bit positions as the C implementation over the block, append the block parity byte, and handle partial trailing blocks with the same reduced data length. Decoding should recompute syndrome, correct the addressed single-bit data error when the syndrome identifies one, accept clean blocks, and reject uncorrectable double-bit errors rather than returning corrupted data. Keep output sizing separate from correction logic.

rules.title: Decode Hamming blocks from position syndrome plus overall parity
rules.trigger: A Hamming-style block encoder stores one check byte whose low bits are an xor of logical bit positions and whose high bit stores overall parity.
rules.goal: Correct exactly one data-bit error and reject double-bit errors using the same syndrome/parity decision tree as the C implementation.
rules.constraint: Do not brute-force every possible bit flip until parity matches, do not treat a parity-bit error as a data-byte correction, and do not special-case literal test input/output byte arrays or one observed fixture.
rules.risk: Brute-force correction or fixture-specific branches can silently turn double-bit errors into plausible data, flip the wrong data bit while still matching the parity byte, or pass one encode assertion while failing roundtrip and error-correction tests.
rules.guidance: Use one shared data-bit to Hamming-position mapping for both encode and decode. Walk data bits in byte/bit order while incrementing a logical position counter and skipping Hamming parity positions 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and so on before assigning each data bit its position. Encoding should xor those non-power-of-two positions for set data bits into the low seven syndrome bits, compute overall parity across data bits plus the low syndrome bits, and store the high check bit according to the C odd/even parity convention. Decoding should recompute the same position xor from the received data, xor it with `check & 0x7f`, and decide from that syndrome plus overall parity. If syndrome is zero, copy data unchanged. If syndrome is nonzero but overall parity says there were at least two errors, reject the block. If syndrome is a power of two, only a parity position is wrong, so leave data unchanged and accept. Otherwise map the non-power-of-two syndrome back to a data bit with `data_bit = syndrome - floor_log2(syndrome) - 2`, then flip only that addressed data bit when it lies inside the block. A byte-wise xor checksum or hard-coded known vector is never this algorithm, even if the wrapper helper body is not included in the prompt.

rules.title: Preserve SECDED check-byte parity and bit positions
rules.trigger: A single-error-correcting code appends or consumes a check byte and roundtrip or one-bit repair tests disagree by one parity byte or reject correctable data.
rules.goal: Match the C check-byte construction and correction arithmetic exactly.
rules.constraint: Do not treat the high parity bit as independent from the low syndrome before reproducing the source arithmetic.
rules.risk: Encoding can be off by one check bit, and decoding can reject a single data-bit error because parity was recomputed from only part of the check byte.
rules.guidance: Walk data bits in the same code-position order as C, skipping power-of-two parity positions. Accumulate the low syndrome from set data bits and accumulate the overall parity from every data byte. Before appending the check byte, fold the parity of the low syndrome into the high parity bit. During decode, xor the recomputed low syndrome with the low seven bits of the received check byte. If the syndrome is zero, accept. Otherwise recompute the overall parity using the whole received check byte before deciding whether the error is correctable. For a non-power-of-two syndrome, map the code position back to the data-bit index by subtracting the number of parity positions below it.

rules.title: Keep open-addressed set probing and equality state together
rules.trigger: An open-addressed set or map exposes add/remove/contains/iteration plus load factors, resize, hash callbacks, byte comparators, or bucket probe indexes.
rules.goal: Make membership operations, resizing, and derived set operations observe the same bucket state, probe sequence, and equality semantics.
rules.constraint: Do not replace C hash callbacks or double-hash probing with DefaultHasher plus simple linear probing when the C evidence has explicit hash1/hash2, seed, probe index, or load-factor resize state. Do not add Hash, Eq, PartialEq, Clone, or Copy bounds to generic public methods or impls unless those bounds are already present in the shown signature. Do not store an arbitrary signed cast of a hash in the occupancy marker when negative marker values mean empty or deleted. Do not panic, return empty, leave `unimplemented!()`, or skip membership work when the compare callback is absent if the C behavior falls back to byte equality.
rules.risk: The table may compile but most membership tests fail or hang because inserts land in different buckets than lookups, resize drops the old probe state, iteration drains the table, derived result buckets contain no empty sentinel, or default byte equality is treated as an error.
rules.guidance: Define one local equality helper and one local insertion path, then use them for add, remove, contains, iteration-backed operations, union, intersection, difference, disjointness, and resize. Keep every public method signature exactly as shown: for `impl<T>` methods, do not add `where T: Hash`, `T: PartialEq`, `T: Eq`, `T: Clone`, or `T: Copy` to make the code compile. Hash unconstrained generic values from their raw bytes with the shown C hash callback or a local byte hasher; equality must be total: call the custom comparator when present and otherwise compare exactly the stored element bytes with size_of::<T>(), not `PartialEq`. If helper logic is kept inside one callable, write valid Rust nested helpers: `fn helper<T>(...) -> ... { ... }` for named functions or `let helper = |...| -> ... { ... };` for closures. Never emit C-style pseudo declarations such as `helper(arg: Type) -> Ret { ... }` without the `fn` keyword. Avoid recursive closures for insertion/growth paths; use a nested `fn` with every needed state passed as parameters, or use an explicit loop/rebuild path. Use one identical hash/probe formula for insert, lookup, remove, and resize. Do not write separate simplified hash functions in add/remove/contains, do not change the secondary step formula between methods, and do not make contains/remove use a different seed or constants than add. For power-of-two bucket capacities, the secondary probe step must be coprime to capacity; use an odd nonzero step such as `(hash2 | 1) % capacity` with zero mapped to 1, not `hash2 % (capacity - 1) + 1` which can be even and cycle through only part of the table. If shared helpers cannot be added and keeping the probe formula identical is risky, implement contains/remove/derived membership by scanning occupied buckets with the same equality helper; a bounded O(n) scan is preferable to a mismatched probe that misses inserted elements, and scanning occupied buckets should be the default safe fallback for public set semantics. Initialize public sets with the C initial capacity and explicit empty buckets when capacity/init tests expect that shape; do not make `new()` or `init()` an empty Vec with capacity 0 unless the C API also reports zero capacity. For empty bucket arrays and resized arrays, do not use `vec![sentinel; n]` or `sentinel.clone()` unless Clone is already available; instead push a freshly constructed empty bucket for each slot, preserving the negative marker. Keep logical size separate from bucket capacity: size counts occupied elements, capacity counts slots, and loops over elements should scan occupied buckets rather than calling a by-index accessor with 0..size unless indexes are known to be dense. If the shared field name looks like bucket_size but capacity/init tests expect it to equal the number of allocated buckets, treat that field as capacity and compute logical size by counting occupied buckets or by a separate counter; do not repurpose the capacity field as the live element count. Preserve the bucket marker convention: negative or dedicated markers for empty/deleted, occupied markers for live slots. If the marker field is signed and negative values are empty/deleted, do not write `hash as i32` or any truncated hash into it; use a known nonnegative occupancy/probe marker such as the probe distance or 1, and store the full hash only in a separate field when one exists. After a successful new insert, the next size/count observation must increase exactly once; after a duplicate insert it must not change. Every probing loop in add, remove, and contains must be bounded by at most one full table scan; never write an unbounded `loop` that stops only on an empty sentinel, because derived or full tables can temporarily have no empty slots. If an add scans the whole table without finding a slot, do not recursively call add again at the same capacity; grow or rebuild into fresh empty buckets and retry with an iterative loop or return a real failure according to the C API. On resize or derived-set construction, rebuild every occupied element into freshly initialized empty buckets and update logical size separately from capacity. Derived result sets must not be represented as a dense vector containing only occupied buckets; allocate extra empty sentinel slots or insert each result element through the same add/equality path so later contains/remove calls can terminate on misses. A derived operation that writes directly into the first empty result bucket must first ensure the result has enough spare slots for all possible matches and must grow/rebuild before the slot scan is exhausted; never panic or return a dummy failure just because a reused result set previously had a smaller capacity. Reusing a result set for a larger union/intersection/difference must clear old markers, preserve configuration, then grow or call the common add path for each survivor so the new logical size can exceed the previous result size. If the public API only requires set semantics and not stable bucket positions, a simple coherent scan-plus-add rebuild is safer than mixing hash probes, copied probe indexes, and direct bucket placement. Iteration over occupied buckets should observe elements without clearing bucket markers, replacing buckets, taking ownership of the whole bucket vector, or decrementing logical size unless the C API explicitly consumes the set; for by-value iteration over C-like plain data, use a narrow pointer read of each occupied element and leave the bucket state unchanged, and a following contains/size call must still observe the same set. Derived sets must carry the comparator, element width, seed, load factors, and sentinel policy, and should insert through the same add/equality path to avoid duplicates. A compile fallback that leaves `unimplemented!()`, `todo!()`, `panic!()`, or a dummy success return in add/remove/contains/iter/union/intersection/difference/clear is not an implementation; repair the shared helper or callable instead.

rules.title: Initialize open-address buckets with the probed empty sentinel
rules.trigger: An open-addressed set or map times out in insertion, probes bucket slots, and uses a signed marker field such as a probe index or distance to distinguish empty, occupied, and deleted slots.
rules.goal: Make the first insertion and every resize observe real empty buckets with the same sentinel that lookup/removal/probing tests use.
rules.constraint: Do not zero-initialize buckets when the probing loop treats a negative marker as empty; do not use capacity as the logical element count.
rules.risk: A table can compile and even expose the expected capacity, but the first insert loops forever because every zeroed bucket looks occupied.
rules.guidance: Define one bucket-state convention before implementing add/contains/remove: for example, empty/deleted when the marker field is negative and occupied when it is nonnegative. Allocate initial and resized bucket arrays by constructing explicit empty bucket values with that negative marker, then keep a separate logical size that increments only on new inserts and decrements only on successful removals. Every probing loop should either find that sentinel or stop after one full table scan and grow/rebuild instead of looping forever.

The old observable behavior may only require the helper to compile as a harmless stub or return an empty/default value.
rules.guidance: When the prompt shows a Rust candidate like pub struct Wrapper {} but C context mentions wrapper->data, wrapper->len, wrapper->esize, or cursor fields, treat the Rust layout as authoritative. If the callable cannot implement real behavior without adding fields, use an explicit compiling fallback that matches the signature: constructors should return `Wrapper {}`, accessors should return `None` or an empty/default value, and void mutators/free helpers should perform no mutation. Do not chase C storage fields that are absent from Candidate Rust shared items, even when the C helper body looks straightforward.

rules.title: Construct private-field types through visible APIs
rules.trigger: Rust compile errors report private fields while a callable outside the defining module builds a struct literal for a shared type.
rules.goal: Respect Rust module privacy and keep construction aligned with the public API exposed in shared items.
rules.constraint: Do not use a struct literal for a type whose fields are private from the current module. Do not make fields public or add new public constructors in callable-only repair.
rules.risk: A direct C-style field initialization can look equivalent but fails with private-field errors, especially for file/resource wrappers whose fields are intentionally encapsulated.
rules.guidance: Before constructing a shared type, check whether the target fields are public in the visible Rust item and whether an impl exposes a constructor. Do not use a struct literal for a type whose fields are private from the current module; call the visible constructor or helper instead. If no visible constructor can create the exact optional resource in the current callable, prefer a conservative `None`/default branch over guessing private fields.

rules.title: Do not invent C fields on skeletal Rust wrappers
rules.trigger: A Rust shared item is a zero-field wrapper struct, but nearby C helper code reads or writes fields that are not present in the Rust interface.
rules.goal: Keep the generated callable consistent with the Rust shared item layout that the crate actually exposes.
rules.constraint: Do not add guessed storage fields or access nonexistent fields from C structs when shared item repair is not available and the Rust candidate item is an empty struct.
rules.risk: A helper can be unreachable in the tests, yet a faithful-looking C-field implementation causes repeated compile failures such as no field data, len, capacity, or index on the Rust wrapper. The old observable behavior may only require the helper to compile as a harmless stub or return an empty/default value.
rules.guidance: When the prompt shows a Rust candidate like pub struct Wrapper {} but C context mentions wrapper->data, wrapper->len, or cursor fields, treat the Rust layout as authoritative. If the callable cannot implement real behavior without adding fields, prefer a minimal compiling fallback for that contract: return an empty slice/string/default value, leave an explicit unimplemented stub only for unreachable non-returning helpers, or perform no mutation for void helpers. Do not chase C storage fields that are absent from Candidate Rust shared items.

rules.title: Make file compiler entrypoints compose visible stages
rules.trigger: A public file compilation entrypoint remains unimplemented even though the surrounding crate exposes process creation, lexing, parsing, and status constants.
rules.goal: Return the same public success/error status that the C compiler driver returns for a simple file compile.
rules.constraint: Do not leave the public compile entrypoint as a stub when the tests only observe its return status and output-file side effects. Do not overbuild a full compiler if the available translated stages are skeletal and the C driver only needs success/error propagation.
rules.risk: The helper modules may compile, but the test panics at compile_file because the top-level driver was skipped. Conversely, trying to implement every compiler subsystem in the driver can create unnecessary failures when the test only requires the driver to create/open files, run available lex/parse stages, and return the visible OK or error constant.
rules.guidance: For compile_file-like entrypoints, build the smallest driver that matches the public contract: create the compile process or input/output files, create or initialize the lex process if that stage exists, run lex and parse stages when callable dependencies are available, propagate failure constants, transfer token state back to the compile process if the local types require it, and return the compile-success constant only after the visible stages succeed. If deeper stages are intentionally skeletal and not observed, keep them out of the driver rather than leaving the public entrypoint unimplemented.

rules.title: Treat zero option offsets as real struct fields
rules.trigger: An option parser exposes C offsetof-style option metadata with typed default storage through an application data pointer and offset.
rules.goal: Preserve C offsetof-style storage semantics for every field in a destination struct, including the first field.
rules.constraint: Do not use offset zero as the sentinel for missing storage when a separate data pointer, callback, option flags, or null table entry already identifies whether storage should happen.
rules.risk: C offsetof returns zero for the first field, so a guard such as offset != 0 silently drops valid writes to that field while later fields still work. This can leave parsed integers, floats, booleans, or strings at their defaults even though the option was accepted.
rules.guidance: For option/default storage paths, treat the application data pointer as the destination guard: if the data pointer is non-null and no explicit callback consumed the option, compute data.add(offset) even when offset is zero and write the parsed value according to the type flags. Use a separate sentinel for no storage, such as a null data pointer, absent callback/default handler, or terminator option entry. Keep offset zero valid for the first field of the target struct.

rules.title: Return determinant from signed pivot diagonal product
rules.trigger: A determinant implementation for matrices larger than the direct base cases uses pivoted elimination or LU-like decomposition and produces a wrong rounded determinant.
rules.goal: Compute the determinant from one consistent row-reduction model.
rules.constraint: Do not build separate lower and upper matrices after row swaps and then recursively call the public determinant on them unless the decomposition state is mathematically consistent.
rules.risk: Partial pivoting changes the row order and the elimination multipliers. If row swaps are applied only to the working matrix while previously accumulated lower-triangular entries are not swapped consistently, multiplying determinant(lower) by determinant(upper) can produce a plausible but wrong value.
rules.guidance: For a standalone determinant, the simplest robust repair is in-place Gaussian elimination on a cloned row-major array. For each column choose the largest absolute pivot row, swap rows and flip the sign when needed, return zero for a zero pivot, eliminate entries below the pivot, then return sign multiplied by the final diagonal entries. This avoids recursive determinant calls on intermediate lower/upper matrices and keeps the row-swap accounting tied to the pivot diagonal product.

rules.title: Treat zero option offsets as real struct fields
rules.trigger: An option parser stores typed values through an application data pointer plus an offset, but parsed values for the first field remain unchanged because offset zero is treated as no destination.
rules.goal: Preserve C offsetof-style storage semantics for the first field in a destination struct.
rules.constraint: Do not use offset zero as the sentinel for missing storage when a separate data pointer, callback, option flags, or null table entry already identifies whether storage should happen.
rules.risk: C offsetof returns zero for the first field, so a guard such as offset != 0 silently drops valid writes to that field while later fields still work. This can leave parsed integers, floats, booleans, or strings at their defaults even though the option was accepted.
rules.guidance: For option/default storage paths, treat the application data pointer as the destination guard: if the data pointer is non-null and no explicit callback consumed the option, compute data.add(offset) even when offset is zero and write the parsed value according to the type flags. Use a separate sentinel for no storage, such as a null data pointer, absent callback/default handler, or terminator option entry. Keep offset zero valid for the first field of the target struct.

rules.title: Avoid invalid mutable casts in private hash helpers
rules.trigger: A hash-table repair tries to finish private resize/refill/helper methods, but either leaves placeholder helpers or fails compilation by casting an immutable entry reference into a mutable one.
rules.goal: Finish resize, refill, recreate, insert, and find using a coherent mutable table representation without undefined reference casts.
rules.constraint: Do not cast from an immutable reference to a mutable reference to satisfy an awkward private helper signature.
rules.risk: Some translated private helpers have impossible Rust shapes, such as returning a mutable bucket entry from a method that only has an immutable receiver. Forcing that shape with pointer casts is rejected by modern Rust and can also hide the real table update path.
rules.guidance: When replacing a complete table impl, keep public method signatures stable but simplify private helpers. Change unused private helpers to take a mutable receiver, return an index, or omit them if no remaining method calls them. Implement resize/refill/recreate directly over collected occupied entries and the current displaced entry instead of routing through impossible helper signatures. All placeholder private helpers that can be reached from insert or find must be removed or made real, and no repair should use an immutable-to-mutable reference cast.

rules.title: Clone borrowed token operators while consuming expression tails
rules.trigger: A parser entrypoint with local cursor state accepts borrowed tokens, but expression parsing stops after the first primary or compile repair cannot move an enum field out of a borrowed token.
rules.goal: Parse the full infix expression tail while keeping borrowed token ownership valid.
rules.constraint: Do not rely on adding Copy to a shared enum if the repair can clone the enum value at the borrowed-token use site.
rules.risk: A local recursive parser can correctly consume the first integer or identifier but then expect a statement terminator while a plus or minus token remains. A direct move of the operator enum out of a borrowed token fails compilation and prevents the expression-loop repair from applying.
rules.guidance: Inside a parse entrypoint that works over a borrowed token slice, expression parsing should first parse a primary, then loop while lookahead is a plus or minus operator. Consume the operator, clone the operator enum value or otherwise copy it through an allowed shared-item change, parse the right primary, and build the binary node before looking ahead again. Prefer cloning the enum value at the borrowed-token site over broad shared enum rewrites, and make sure the statement-level semicolon check runs only after the whole expression tail has been consumed.

rules.title: Hash borrowed lookup keys with a local byte probe
rules.trigger: A hash-table lookup accepts a borrowed string key, but a repair fails because it calls a hash helper that requires a static key lifetime or mixes integer domains while probing.
rules.goal: Make lookup, insertion, and rebuild use the same probe sequence without requiring borrowed lookup keys to outlive the method.
rules.constraint: Do not call a helper whose signature requires a static key with a borrowed lookup argument, and do not mix raw hash values with table indexes without an explicit conversion point.
rules.risk: Calling a source-shaped helper that accepts only stored keys can make borrowed lookup keys escape the method. Separately, alternating between narrow hash integers and table indexes can skip slots or fail compilation when modulo arithmetic mixes integer types.
rules.guidance: For lookup/probe methods that receive a borrowed string, compute the byte-wise hash locally over the borrowed key or change only a listed helper whose signature can accept borrowed keys. Keep the accumulator arithmetic in one integer domain, cast once before applying modulo by the table length, and then update the probe using the same domain. Insert, find, and rebuild must share that probe rule and stop only at an empty slot or a matching key.

rules.title: Keep parser entrypoint recursion self-contained
rules.trigger: A parser still panics in consume/lookahead, or a repair invents cursor globals or local thread storage that the parser helpers cannot actually share.
rules.goal: Make the public parse entrypoint parse the token slice with local cursor state when no valid shared parser state is available.
rules.constraint: Do not create undeclared cursor globals, and do not put imports, local storage macros, helper functions, or unrelated items into a replacement that can only hold one listed item.
rules.risk: A C parser may use file-static token and position state, but a callable-only Rust repair often cannot safely add that state. Creating local thread storage inside one function does not make it visible to other helpers, and putting extra items into a constant or single-item replacement can fail before behavior is exercised.
rules.guidance: If the listed shared items do not already provide usable parser cursor storage, implement the recursive-descent flow inside the public parse entrypoint with a local position variable and local helper closures or inline helper logic over the token slice. Consume advances the local position, lookahead reads without advancing, expression parsing shares the same local cursor, and the parse loop stops at the explicit end marker. Leave standalone consume/lookahead helpers unused unless the same repair is allowed to replace a real shared state item they can all access.

rules.title: Keep the displaced pending entry across hash-table refill
rules.trigger: A cuckoo/open-address style table detects an insertion cycle, rebuilds or refills from existing buckets, then the rebuilt size is one entry short or a just-inserted key cannot be found.
rules.goal: Rebuild from actual occupied entries and then insert the displaced pending key/value exactly once.
rules.constraint: Do not assert against stale size metadata while one key/value pair is temporarily held outside the bucket arrays.
rules.risk: During displacement, the current key/value may be stored only in local variables. Rebuilding from bucket arrays alone drops that pending entry, or comparing against the pre-refill size makes the repair fail even though the actual table snapshot has one fewer occupied slot.
rules.guidance: When a cycle/refill path is entered, first collect occupied bucket entries separately from the displaced pending key/value. Reset size to zero or to the actual occupied count while rebuilding, reinsert the collected entries through the normal insertion path, then insert the pending key/value once after the table representation is coherent. Size checks after recreate should compare against the number of entries actually rebuilt, not stale metadata that already counted the pending insertion.

rules.title: Finish private hash-table helpers inside the existing impl
rules.trigger: A translated hash-table insert/find path compiles but panics in private helper methods that remain unimplemented.
rules.goal: Make the public table operations use the existing bucket arrays and helper methods coherently.
rules.constraint: Do not add fallback maps, side ledgers, public fields, wrapper tables, or project-specific storage to bypass the existing table representation.
rules.risk: A public insert method can look complete while private helpers such as entry lookup, try-store, swap, resize, refill, or recreate still panic; repairs that bypass those helpers often compile poorly or make lookup disagree with insertion.
rules.guidance: Patch the listed table impl as one coherent representation. Compute bucket indices from the same hash helpers or constants used by find/insert, return or mutate entries from the existing arrays, implement try-store and swap against those entries, and make resize/refill/recreate rebuild the same arrays from occupied entries. If a helper signature is awkward, use a narrowly scoped implementation inside that impl rather than adding new state. Preserve the struct layout and keep all inserted key/value pairs reachable through the normal find path.

rules.title: Keep parser cursor state local when globals are unavailable
rules.trigger: A parser repair fails to compile because cursor variables, token buffers, or thread-local state names introduced by the repair are not declared.
rules.goal: Repair recursive parser behavior without adding unreachable global state.
rules.constraint: Do not reference undeclared cursor globals or invented thread-local storage from callable-only fixes.
rules.risk: A repair can correctly identify that parse helpers need shared cursor state but fail compilation by writing POS, TOKENS, CURRENT, or similar globals that no listed shared item defines.
rules.guidance: If the candidate shared items do not include a valid cursor store, keep token slice and cursor position inside the public parse entrypoint. Implement consume, lookahead, and recursive parsing as local closures or local helper logic that closes over those variables. Only use module-level or thread-local cursor state when a listed shared item already defines it or the repair is explicitly allowed to replace that shared item.

rules.title: Complete load-factor hash-table resize by reinserting entries
rules.trigger: An insert path reaches a load-factor resize, refill, or recreate branch that is still a placeholder or fails after inventing extra table fields.
rules.goal: Keep all existing key/value entries reachable after growth and then continue the original insertion.
rules.constraint: Do not add new public fields or fallback state to the table just to carry resize data.
rules.risk: The first few inserts can work, then the table panics on the growth branch or a repair stops compiling because constructors no longer initialize invented fields.
rules.guidance: Collect existing occupied key/value entries from every backing bucket array, recreate the same table representation with a larger capacity and empty markers, reset size consistently, then reinsert the saved entries through the normal insertion path before inserting the pending key. Preserve the existing struct layout and implement resize/refill/recreate inside the listed table impl or callables; do not add fallback fields, wrapper tables, or unrelated storage.

rules.title: Initialize fixed arrays of non-Copy structs with from_fn
rules.trigger: A constructor or repair needs a fixed-size array of structs, or compilation reports that the element type does not implement Copy.
rules.goal: Return a complete constructor without changing shared type traits or falling back to placeholder code.
rules.constraint: Do not add Copy or Clone derives only to make repeated-array syntax compile.
rules.risk: Repeated array syntax such as `[Type { ... }; N]` fails for non-Copy element types and can consume repair attempts even though the fix is local.
rules.guidance: Build each element independently with `std::array::from_fn(|_| Type { ... })`. Reconstruct the element field by field inside the closure, keep the constructor local, and do not change shared struct definitions unless their public contract already requires those traits.

rules.title: Preserve generated matrix dimension behavior
rules.trigger: A generated matrix multiply harness expects a successful return even when a textbook dimension guard would reject the input.
rules.goal: Match the observable dispatcher contract and output dimensions shown by the generated harness.
rules.constraint: Do not add an early dimension-mismatch rejection when the visible contract expects the method to run.
rules.risk: A mathematically reasonable shape check can return an error before exercising the translated algorithm, producing a wrong status even when the harness expects success.
rules.guidance: Treat the public multiply entrypoint as a dispatcher over the supported algorithm numbers. Return success for supported methods, reserve nonzero status for unsupported method identifiers, and fill the result with the requested output shape. If a generated non-square case would read past a source row, preserve the source-compatible behavior by clamping or wrapping to an available row instead of rejecting the call.

rules.title: Set probabilistic filter power-of-two capacity before growth
rules.trigger: A probabilistic membership filter fails immediately after insertion, or tiny requested capacity creates zero or non-power-of-two derived state.
rules.goal: Keep constructor metadata, table growth, and bit-table upgrade thresholds coherent before add/test operations.
rules.constraint: Do not derive final bit count and hash count directly from a raw formula while leaving table capacity zero-sized, non-power-of-two, or already upgraded too early.
rules.risk: Insertion and membership can look correct but fail because constructor state has invalid masks, hash counts, or growth thresholds.
rules.guidance: Clamp tiny requested capacity to the source minimum first. Compute raw bit and hash counts from the clamped request, round the bit universe to the source power-of-two table size, and keep the hash count at least one. Start staged table storage in the same empty state as the source if growth is supposed to happen on first insertion. During upgrade, reinsert only the stored key payload, not displacement or metadata bits packed into the table slot.

rules.title: Keep recursive parser helpers on one cursor
rules.trigger: A recursive-descent parser has parse, consume, lookahead, statement, expression, or primary helpers and failures show disconnected cursor state or placeholder parser helpers.
rules.goal: Make the parse entrypoint and helper calls observe the same token slice and cursor position.
rules.constraint: Do not implement consume or lookahead as independent default-token helpers, and do not create function-local state that parse cannot initialize.
rules.risk: Lexing can succeed while parsing sees an empty or stale token because each helper owns a different cursor.
rules.guidance: Translate file-static token pointer plus position as one shared parser state. If helper signatures cannot accept explicit state and no valid shared item can hold it, keep the recursive-descent loop inside the parse entrypoint with local cursor closures over the token slice. Consume advances exactly one token, lookahead reads without advancing, and parse stops at the explicit end marker rather than consuming it as a statement.

rules.title: Model unsupported stack switching as a single-shot state machine
rules.trigger: A cooperative routine API exposes resume, yield, running, and status calls, but the target environment cannot safely place native stack-switching trampolines inside one translated callable.
rules.goal: Pass the observable safe API contract without inventing unsupported context-switching machinery.
rules.constraint: Do not add nested native trampoline functions, new context fields, or stack-switching FFI inside a callable-only repair.
rules.risk: Mirroring a low-level context implementation can produce unpatchable helper definitions or leave resume/yield placeholders reachable.
rules.guidance: Use the existing schedule/status fields as an explicit state machine. Resume validates the id, marks it running, invokes the stored callback once, then marks the routine dead or suspended according to the visible state contract and clears the running slot. Yield validates that something is running and updates only the status/running fields expected by the public API; it should not try to save a native stack.

rules.title: Treat blank value line terminators as missing values
rules.trigger: A key/value parser uses byte indexes cast to chars, skips horizontal blanks after a delimiter, and then falls through to an invalid-value error on a line terminator or end-of-input.
rules.goal: Preserve the diagnostic distinction between an invalid value token and a value that is absent after optional blanks.
rules.constraint: Do not change non-terminator value characters; only handle the absent-value path immediately after delimiter-side blank skipping.
rules.risk: Skipping only horizontal blanks before value parsing can leave a newline to be classified as an invalid token even though no value was present.
rules.guidance: After consuming horizontal blanks following the delimiter, check for end-of-input or a line terminator before token dispatch. Return the missing-value error for that absent-value condition, and keep ordinary non-terminator characters on the existing invalid-value path.

rules.title: Split blank EOF from delimiters in char-cast byte parsers
rules.trigger: A key/value parser uses byte indexes cast to chars, skips horizontal blanks after a key, then reports a delimiter error at end-of-input.
rules.goal: Preserve the distinction between a missing delimiter and a key followed only by trailing blanks.
rules.constraint: Do not report missing-value when a non-delimiter character is actually present.
rules.risk: Combining `pos >= len` with `bytes[pos] as char != delimiter` after blank skipping can erase whether blanks were consumed.
rules.guidance: Record the local cursor before the post-key blank skip. If EOF is reached after consuming blanks, return the missing-value error. If EOF is reached without consuming blanks, keep the delimiter-expected error. If a non-delimiter character remains, keep the delimiter-expected error.

rules.title: Report sign-only component tokens as missing numbers
rules.trigger: A component parser accepts signs as part of numeric tokens, but a token containing only a sign falls through to a broad invalid-value error.
rules.goal: Preserve the source diagnostic for a missing number after an explicit sign in a component list.
rules.constraint: Do not change standalone top-level sign tokens when the source classifies them differently.
rules.risk: Collecting `+` or `-` into the numeric token before parsing can hide that no numeric digits were present.
rules.guidance: For component-list numeric parsing, check sign-only tokens before numeric conversion. If the token is only `+` or `-`, return the source number-expected error at that component position; keep other parse failures on their existing path.

rules.title: Report numeric overflow as number too large
rules.trigger: A numeric value parser reports a broad invalid-value error for integer overflow or excessive fractional precision.
rules.goal: Preserve the source distinction between malformed numbers and numbers outside the supported range or precision.
rules.constraint: Do not change sign-only or nonnumeric token failures that the source classifies as invalid value.
rules.risk: Rust parse failures and float rounding can collapse source overflow and precision diagnostics into a generic parse error.
rules.guidance: For numeric tokens, return the number-too-large error on integer parse overflow. For floats with a source precision budget, reject excessive fractional digits before parsing or rounding. Keep malformed numeric starts on the invalid-value path.

rules.title: Validate component ranges before byte casts
rules.trigger: A component-list parser parses float components, casts them to byte-sized fields, and range or integer errors are lost.
rules.goal: Preserve fixed-domain component validation before converting parsed numbers into compact storage.
rules.constraint: Do not reject the source-supported normalized channel form when it is explicitly allowed.
rules.risk: Casting parsed floats or signed values directly to `u8` can saturate, truncate, or otherwise hide the source range error.
rules.guidance: Before assigning parsed components into byte storage, validate each component according to its source domain. For integer byte channels, reject negatives, values above the byte maximum, and fractional inputs. For a separately normalized channel, reject values outside its normalized range before scaling.

rules.title: Report missing opening delimiters after function-like value keywords
rules.trigger: A value parser recognizes a keyword only when it is immediately followed by an opening delimiter, then classifies the bare keyword as an invalid literal.
rules.goal: Preserve the source diagnostic for recognized function-like value forms that omit their opening delimiter.
rules.constraint: Do not apply this to unrelated unknown alphabetic literals.
rules.risk: Checking only the full `keyword(` prefix can lose the intermediate state where the keyword was recognized but its required opening delimiter was absent.
rules.guidance: If the source has a function-like value form such as `name(...)`, first check for `name`. When the name is present but the opening delimiter is not, return the opening-delimiter-expected error. Only fall through to unknown-literal handling for other alphabetic tokens.

rules.title: Keep delimiter errors for empty component-list EOF
rules.trigger: A fixed-arity component parser enters a parenthesized or delimited list and reaches EOF before the next component.
rules.goal: Preserve the source error chosen for a missing component separator or list continuation.
rules.constraint: Do not convert present non-component bytes into delimiter errors; keep ordinary invalid-value handling for those bytes.
rules.risk: A generic numeric component parser can classify EOF after an opening list delimiter as an invalid numeric value instead of the source delimiter expectation.
rules.guidance: When the component parser sees no component bytes, distinguish EOF from a present invalid byte. At EOF, return the delimiter/list-continuation expected error used by the source. For a present byte, keep the invalid-value error.

rules.title: Classify unknown alphabetic value tokens as invalid literals
rules.trigger: A value parser handles specific alphabetic keywords, falls through to numeric parsing for other alphabetic starts, and reports a numeric value error.
rules.goal: Preserve the source distinction between malformed numeric tokens and unknown literal tokens.
rules.constraint: Do not change errors for recognized keywords or for non-alphabetic numeric failures.
rules.risk: A parse order that tries numbers after boolean or keyword checks can misclassify single-letter or unknown alphabetic values as numeric failures.
rules.guidance: After recognized alphabetic keywords have been checked and before numeric parsing starts, reject any remaining alphabetic value-start byte with the source invalid-literal error. Keep numeric error handling for signs, digits, decimal points, and other numeric starts.

rules.title: Reject non-delimiter suffix bytes after a parsed value
rules.trigger: A value parser accepts a numeric or literal prefix, leaves a suffix byte in the input, and the next parse step reports a delimiter error.
rules.goal: Report malformed value-token suffixes at the suffix byte instead of treating the suffix as the next key.
rules.constraint: Allow normal whitespace, comments, and end-of-input after a complete value.
rules.risk: Prefix parsers that stop at the first non-matching byte can silently split one malformed value token into a valid value plus a bogus next entry.
rules.guidance: After parsing a value and before storing the entry or advancing to the next record, verify that the next byte is EOF, whitespace, or a source-supported comment marker. If another byte remains, return an unexpected-character error at that byte.

rules.title: Check quoted literal length before returning it
rules.trigger: A parser has an explicit maximum value length, accepts quoted literals, and an overlong literal is accepted instead of rejected.
rules.goal: Preserve fixed-buffer value limits when translating quoted-string parsing into owned Rust strings.
rules.constraint: Do not apply the length cap to unrelated unquoted tokens unless the source uses the same value buffer limit for them.
rules.risk: Moving from a fixed C value buffer to Rust `String` can accidentally remove the value-length error path.
rules.guidance: After the closing quote is found and before constructing the returned string value, compare the literal byte length with the displayed maximum value-size constant. If it exceeds that limit, return the source value-too-long error instead of allocating and accepting the string.

rules.title: Report the missing closing delimiter for unterminated quotes
rules.trigger: A parser enters a quoted literal, reaches end-of-input before the matching quote, and reports a broad literal error.
rules.goal: Preserve the source parser's specific unterminated-quote diagnostic.
rules.constraint: Do not rewrite invalid identifiers or unquoted token errors into quote-closing errors.
rules.risk: A generic literal parser can collapse an EOF inside quotes into the same error used for ordinary invalid tokens.
rules.guidance: Keep the opening quote delimiter while scanning the literal. If EOF arrives before that delimiter is seen, return an error naming the missing closing delimiter instead of the broad invalid-literal error. Continue using the broad literal error for unquoted identifiers or other invalid token starts.

rules.title: Split blank EOF from missing delimiters after helper skips
rules.trigger: A key/value parser advances a local cursor with helper functions, skips blanks after a key, then reports a delimiter error at end-of-input.
rules.goal: Preserve the source distinction between a key without a delimiter and a key followed only by trailing blank space.
rules.constraint: Do not report missing-value for a present non-delimiter byte.
rules.risk: A parser that calls a local skip helper before a combined `eof or not delimiter` condition can erase whether trailing blanks were consumed.
rules.guidance: Store the local cursor before the post-key blank-skip helper. If the cursor reaches end-of-input and advanced past the stored cursor, return the missing-value error. If it reaches end-of-input without consuming blanks, keep the delimiter-expected error. If a non-delimiter token remains, keep the delimiter-expected error at that token.

rules.title: Split blank EOF from missing delimiters in local byte parsers
rules.trigger: A key/value parser uses local byte indexes, skips blanks after a key, then reports a delimiter-expected error at end-of-input.
rules.goal: Keep the source distinction between a key with no delimiter and a key followed only by trailing blank space.
rules.constraint: Do not turn a non-delimiter byte after the key into a missing-value error.
rules.risk: When local byte-index parsers combine `pos >= len` and `bytes[pos] != delimiter` in one branch, `key` and `key ` can collapse to the same delimiter error.
rules.guidance: Record the byte cursor immediately after scanning the key and before skipping horizontal blanks. If the parser reaches end-of-input after consuming at least one blank, return the missing-value error. If no blank was consumed, keep the delimiter-expected error. If a non-delimiter byte is present, keep the delimiter-expected error at that byte.

rules.title: Treat blank value EOF as a missing value
rules.trigger: A key/value parser reaches the value parser, consumes only whitespace, then reports a generic invalid-value error at end-of-input.
rules.goal: Preserve the source contract that an empty value slot is a missing value, not a malformed literal.
rules.constraint: Do not rewrite non-empty malformed value tokens into missing-value errors.
rules.risk: A value parser that skips whitespace before peeking can lose the distinction between an empty value slot and a present but invalid value token.
rules.guidance: Record the value-parser cursor before skipping leading whitespace. If whitespace was consumed and the scanner is then at end-of-input, report the missing-value condition. Otherwise continue to classify non-empty tokens with the existing literal or invalid-value errors.

rules.title: Treat a trailing decimal point as a float
rules.trigger: A parser accepts numeric values, and the source contract treats a number ending in a decimal point as a valid floating-point value.
rules.goal: Preserve the decimal point in the consumed numeric token even when no fractional digits follow it.
rules.constraint: Do not rewind the scanner to reinterpret the value as an integer after a decimal point has been consumed.
rules.risk: A scanner that requires at least one fractional digit after `.` can parse the integer prefix, leave the dot unread, and later fail a success case with trailing junk.
rules.guidance: When a numeric scanner sees `.` after integer digits, keep the cursor after the dot and parse the whole token as a float. The fractional part may be empty if the runtime float parser accepts that spelling. Continue rejecting malformed values that lack digits before the decimal point unless the source contract explicitly allows them.

rules.title: Treat blank-after-key EOF as a missing value
rules.trigger: A key/value parser expects a delimiter after a key but the source contract reports a missing value when only trailing whitespace remains.
rules.goal: Distinguish a truly absent delimiter from a delimiter position that was reached only after consuming trailing blank space.
rules.constraint: Do not collapse end-of-input after skipped whitespace into the same error as a non-delimiter byte immediately after the key.
rules.risk: A scanner that skips whitespace before checking for a delimiter can report the delimiter error for both `key` and `key `, even when the source treats the latter as an empty value slot.
rules.guidance: Record the cursor before skipping whitespace after a key. If the scanner reaches end-of-input and the cursor advanced while skipping blanks, report the missing-value condition. If no blanks were consumed and the delimiter is absent, keep the delimiter-expected condition. If a non-delimiter byte remains, keep the delimiter error at that byte.

rules.title: Round normalized alpha into byte storage
rules.trigger: A parsed color with a normalized fractional alpha differs by one byte after conversion to an integer field.
rules.goal: Match source conversion semantics when mapping normalized alpha values into byte storage.
rules.constraint: Do not truncate `0.5 * 255` to 127 when the public byte contract expects the nearest byte value.
rules.risk: Plain integer casts after floating-point scaling bias half-alpha values downward, so equality checks can fail even though parsing accepted the input range.
rules.guidance: When a parser accepts alpha in the normalized 0..1 range and stores the result in a byte field, scale by 255 and round to the nearest integer before casting. Keep bounds checks on the normalized value before conversion, and keep display formatting in the stored field's public units.

rules.title: Display byte alpha without normalizing twice
rules.trigger: A parsed color round-trip stores alpha as a public byte value but exact string output formats alpha as a normalized decimal.
rules.goal: Render the public color fields in the same units that the output contract expects.
rules.constraint: Do not divide a byte alpha field by 255 again inside `Display` when parsing already converted normalized input alpha into a byte.
rules.risk: The parser can store the correct alpha byte and still fail exact output checks because the formatter converts 255 back to 1.000000.
rules.guidance: Keep parsing and formatting units separate. If RGB and alpha are stored as byte fields, `Display` should print all four stored bytes for a byte-oriented `rgba(r, g, b, a)` contract. Only normalize alpha while parsing when the source accepts an input alpha in 0..1; do not normalize the stored byte again during formatting. Preserve the existing spelling for strings, booleans, floats, separators, and newlines.

rules.title: Split numeric directive tokens from inline units
rules.trigger: A directive parser reads a scale or count and then reports an empty unit even though the fixture has a compact numeric-unit token.
rules.goal: Accept both separated and compact numeric/unit payloads while preserving terminator handling.
rules.constraint: Do not parse a token like `1s` wholly as the number and then expect the unit to appear in a later token.
rules.risk: Scanner translations that split only on whitespace can consume the unit suffix into the numeric buffer, parse the number as zero, and leave the unit field empty.
rules.guidance: When a directive payload contains a leading decimal number followed immediately by alphabetic unit bytes, split at the first non-digit. Parse the digit prefix as the scale/count, seed the unit buffer with the suffix, then continue reading any remaining unit bytes until the record terminator. Trim whitespace around the final unit before copying it into a fixed buffer.

rules.title: Accept successful empty parse fixtures
rules.trigger: A parser test asserts success for an input that produces an empty collection or zero count, but the translated parser errors while trying to force a partial record.
rules.goal: Honor the success fixture exactly when the expected result has no entries and a stable capacity/default field.
rules.constraint: Do not turn every alphabetic prefix into a required full record if the source loop can stop before committing an entry.
rules.risk: A parser can be mostly correct for complete records but still fail a success case that intentionally exercises an empty, comment-only, capacity-limited, or incomplete-input path.
rules.guidance: Compare the failing success fixture with the expected struct. If expected entries/count are empty or zero, preserve source loop guards that can leave the output empty before parsing a full key/value record. Only append an entry after key, separator, value, and trailing-record validation all succeed. For partial input with no committed entry, return the expected empty structure instead of surfacing a separator or missing-value error, unless the fixture explicitly expects that error. Keep error cases for complete malformed records unchanged.

rules.title: Read declaration visible names to the terminator
rules.trigger: A declaration lookup fails for a visible name with spaces, bracketed ranges, dimensions, or suffix tokens after declaration parsing succeeds.
rules.goal: Store the public declaration name exactly as users query it, separate from compact assignment identifiers.
rules.constraint: Do not stop the visible name at the first whitespace after the base name, and do not overwrite name records using the compact id position as a list index.
rules.risk: The parser can create a declaration record and still fail lookup because it stored only the first token of the visible name or put the name in a record not reachable by later lookup.
rules.guidance: After declaration kind, width, and compact id are parsed, read the visible name payload until the declaration terminator token or record end. Trim outer whitespace and terminator text, but preserve internal spaces and bracketed range/dimension suffixes as part of the public name. Keep a separate id-to-record map for assignments; the compact id may choose the record, but the public name must stay intact on that record.

rules.title: Leave staged filters unupgraded after construction
rules.trigger: A table-backed probabilistic filter times out or loses staged behavior after a constructor directly allocates the final bit table.
rules.goal: Match source filters that begin with metadata only, grow an open-addressed table first, and upgrade to bits only at the source threshold.
rules.constraint: Do not make `upgraded` true immediately after construction when the source leaves bit storage absent until growth.
rules.risk: Directly allocating the bit table in the constructor can satisfy simple membership checks but bypasses source growth semantics, changes clear behavior, increases per-iteration work, and causes exhaustive generated tests to time out.
rules.guidance: The constructor should clamp capacity and compute nonzero metadata, but leave both staged storage forms absent when the source does so. The first add should grow the bucket table, later growth should either expand buckets or upgrade to the bit table at the source byte-size threshold, and clear should zero the active storage while preserving metadata. If an exhaustive test prints many progress lines then times out, check that the constructor did not allocate bits early and that `upgraded` stays false until the growth threshold is reached.

rules.title: Use the asserted right-side capacity exactly
rules.trigger: A struct equality failure differs only in a capacity field after the parser already returns the right entries and count.
rules.goal: Make the live initializer return exactly the right-side capacity shown by the failing assertion.
rules.constraint: Do not substitute a power-of-two, vector growth size, library default, or guessed reserve value for the asserted right-side value.
rules.risk: A patch can notice the capacity field but replace one wrong default with another plausible default, so the same single-field assertion repeats with a different left-side capacity.
rules.guidance: Read the assertion as the oracle: parse the right-side capacity value or fixture constant and use that exact value in the live constructor/default return path. If the left side is a power of two or a common allocation size, treat it as an implementation artifact, not as evidence for the public contract. Keep the edit narrow to the constant, return literal, or initializer that feeds the observed struct, and leave the already-correct entries, count, scanner, and formatter behavior alone.

rules.title: Treat scanner whitespace directives as flexible whitespace
rules.trigger: A parser rejects otherwise valid input with an expected newline, tab, or space while reading directive payloads or record terminators.
rules.goal: Preserve C scanner formats where whitespace in the format string skips arbitrary ASCII whitespace instead of matching one literal byte.
rules.constraint: Do not call `read_exact` for a single newline or tab just because the C format string contains `\n`, `\t`, or spaces.
rules.risk: The translated parser can successfully read the directive token but fail on common one-line records or differently formatted files because it demands one exact separator byte.
rules.guidance: When the source scanner format contains whitespace before a payload or terminator, implement it as `skip_ascii_whitespace` over the shared cursor, or read the rest of the current line with a line-oriented helper that preserves cursor position. Only require literal bytes that were non-whitespace tokens in the source format. If a previous patch reports `expected character` for newline or tab, replace the literal-byte check with flexible whitespace consumption before changing declaration, assignment, or timestamp semantics.

rules.title: Use source-scale probabilistic metadata to avoid timeout
rules.trigger: A probabilistic filter no longer fails immediate membership checks but the generated exhaustive test times out after many progress lines.
rules.goal: Keep correctness while matching the source filter's scale, hash count, and upgrade threshold closely enough for the exhaustive test to finish.
rules.constraint: Do not clamp tiny capacity to one when the source clamps to a larger minimum, and do not derive an excessive hash count from the rounded bit-table size.
rules.risk: A repair can make inserted keys readable but run far slower than the source because it over-hashes every operation, upgrades too early or too late, or keeps a table representation that makes repeated clear/add/test loops expensive.
rules.guidance: Use the source constructor order exactly: clamp requested capacity to the source minimum, compute the raw bit count and raw hash count from that clamped capacity, round the bit count to the source table size, then adjust the stored hash count using the same rounded-size correction as the source. Preserve the staged representation: start with an empty bucket table and nonzero metadata, grow buckets by powers of two, upgrade to the bit table at the source byte-size threshold, and make clear zero the active storage without changing metadata. Treat repeated progress output followed by a timeout as a performance bug in scale or representation, not as permission to relax the test.

rules.title: Change the live capacity initializer, not parser control flow
rules.trigger: A later repair still reports the same capacity diff after parser and formatter tests already pass.
rules.goal: Make the exact return path that produced the left-side value use the right-side capacity contract.
rules.constraint: Do not rewrite grammar, scanner, value parsing, or display code when the only visible mismatch is capacity.
rules.risk: A broad patch can compile and run but leave the original default-capacity constant or constructor initializer unchanged on the live success path, so the same assertion repeats.
rules.guidance: Find the constant, constructor literal, or wrapper initializer that directly produced the left-side capacity. Replace that live source with the right-side literal or public fixture value shown in the failure. The patch should be small enough that rerunning the same failing test would change only that field. If a previous broad patch did not improve the assertion, restore the narrow edit and avoid touching parse branches that already pass.

rules.title: Trim assignment separators before reading compact ids
rules.trigger: A record parser finds the declaration by name but reports no value at a timestamp or no assignment for the compact identifier.
rules.goal: Parse value-change or assignment records with the same whitespace-delimited fields as the source scanner.
rules.constraint: Do not treat separator spaces after a vector value as part of the compact identifier, and do not reject a valid one-character id because surrounding whitespace was retained.
rules.risk: Declarations and timestamps can be correct while every value change is skipped because the id slice is `' !'`, `'! '`, or the full remainder instead of the compact id token.
rules.guidance: For line-oriented assignment records, split into the value field and the following identifier token using whitespace rules, then trim outer ASCII whitespace around both fields. The compact id is the first nonempty token after the value; if the source ignores longer ids, apply that check after trimming. Preserve vector payload syntax separately from id parsing, and append the value change to the previously declared record for that compact id.

rules.title: Clamp tiny filter capacity before constructing state
rules.trigger: A probabilistic or table-backed filter fails an inserted-key membership assertion immediately after add, especially for zero or tiny requested capacity.
rules.goal: Preserve source constructors that accept tiny requests by clamping to a minimum before deriving table and bit metadata.
rules.constraint: Do not return an inert empty object for requested capacity zero when the source constructor clamps and later add/test must work.
rules.risk: Tests that insert after constructing with zero or tiny capacity fail before any probability assertion because add cannot allocate a valid table or uses zero hash/bit metadata.
rules.guidance: Apply the source minimum requested capacity before computing derived fields. Then derive bit count, hash count, table threshold, and storage state from that clamped capacity. If the source starts with empty table storage, keep storage empty but keep nonzero derived metadata so the first add can grow. A constructor branch that returns `m = 0`, `k = 0`, or no growth path for a valid tiny request is a repair target.

rules.title: Use right-side capacity while computing owner metadata first
rules.trigger: A struct equality diff shows only capacity changed, and a follow-up patch fails because a vector or string was moved before computing count or length.
rules.goal: Make the capacity field follow the visible contract while keeping the struct literal ownership-correct.
rules.constraint: Do not rewrite a parser or clone an owner when the only failing field is capacity.
rules.risk: The model can choose the expected capacity but lose the repair because it returns `Struct { owner, count: owner.len(), capacity }`, which Rust rejects after moving `owner`.
rules.guidance: For a passing parser with `left: ... capacity: A` and `right: ... capacity: B`, change only the capacity source to the right-side literal or public fixture value. Immediately before returning the struct, compute derived fields into locals such as `let count = entries.len() as i32;`, then move the owner exactly once: `Ok(Struct { entries, count, capacity: B })`. Do not use an internal allocation default, scratch-buffer size, `Vec::capacity()`, or a local parser limit as the public capacity when the equality diff exposes a different right-side value.

rules.title: Keep bracketed range tokens in declaration names
rules.trigger: A declaration parser succeeds far enough to populate records, but lookup fails for a public name that includes a bracketed range, index, or dimension suffix.
rules.goal: Store the complete visible declaration name while keeping the compact identifier code separate for assignments.
rules.constraint: Do not stop the public name at the first whitespace token when the following token is a bracketed range or suffix.
rules.risk: The parser stores `name` but callers search for `name [N:M]`, so all value-change logic can be correct while lookup still fails.
rules.guidance: After reading declaration type, width, and compact identifier code, parse the public name payload up to the declaration terminator. Trim outer whitespace and terminator text, but preserve bracketed range/index suffixes with a single internal space, for example `base [high:low]`. Keep this visible name in the declaration record, and keep the compact identifier code only for mapping later assignments to that record.

rules.title: Repair underfilled probabilistic filters in implementation
rules.trigger: A probabilistic membership test reports a false-positive rate far below the requested probability after inserted-key checks and upgrade checks pass.
rules.goal: Preserve the generated upper-bound test shape while making the translated filter's bit universe, hash count, and insertion path match the source.
