rules.guidance: Translate the mutation itself. For ordered splice/remove operations, clamp the removed range to the current length and drain or shift elements so survivors keep their relative order. For swap-splice/swap-remove operations on an unconstrained Vec<T>, do not use copy_within, clone, or a new trait bound. Use swaps between the removal range and the original tail, or move values through drain/collect/append so ownership is transferred. A safe pattern is: remember the original length, clamp count, swap each destination slot with the corresponding slot from the original tail when order is irrelevant, then truncate to original_len - count. Compute the tail source from the original length before removal, and never remove the target range first and then insert tail elements at the old start index without clamping; after any drain/truncate, the insertion or overwrite index must be at most the current length. If the target range touches or overlaps the tail, move only the actually available tail elements and finish by truncating. Keep out-of-range start/count behavior aligned with the C code, and make capacity helpers separate from logical length changes.

rules.title: Emit both directed contact force updates
rules.trigger: A contact loop accumulates normal and tangential pair forces for two endpoints and stores previous-force state in pair-indexed arrays.
rules.goal: Make every contact visibly update both directed pair slots and both endpoint force accumulators.
rules.constraint: Do not translate a two-endpoint contact as a single directed update plus a comment about C semantics. Do not rely on one equal-and-opposite force write to stand in for the reverse matrix slot or the first endpoint's accumulator. Do not leave the reverse direction hidden behind a helper whose arguments are passed by value.
rules.risk: The code compiles and one endpoint may move, but tests or callers that inspect the other endpoint or the reverse previous-force cell observe zero force because the public loop never executed that directed update.
rules.guidance: In the public contact loop, build an explicit two-call or two-block shape. First compute the forward direction from source endpoint A to destination endpoint B, read and write the `A * count + B` normal/tangent history slot, and add the signed normal plus tangential contribution to B's output force. Then compute the reverse direction from B to A, with the normal vector negated, relative velocity order swapped, destination material/properties taken from A, the history slot changed to `B * count + A`, and the output force write changed to A's accumulator. The reverse block must repeat the same clamping and friction-limit order as the forward block; it is not a cosmetic mirror or a post-processing subtraction. If a helper cannot mutate the previous normal force, previous tangential force, and destination output vector in place, inline the arithmetic twice in the public loop. A correct patch should make both matrix indexes and both endpoint output writes obvious in the generated Rust.

rules.title: Update both pairwise contact output slots
rules.trigger: A pairwise collision/contact/force loop writes normal, tangent, previous-state, or resultant force arrays through output parameters.
rules.goal: Preserve the C side effects for both endpoints and both matrix directions of each pairwise interaction.
rules.constraint: Do not compute only one direction, do not leave either endpoint's resultant force as zero, and do not share one previous-force slot for both endpoints when the C code indexes a matrix by source and destination. Do not stop after writing only `forces[dst]`, `forces[p2]`, or one `normal_forces[src * n + dst]` slot. Do not delegate the real update to a helper whose signature takes previous force or output vectors by value or immutable reference.
rules.risk: The numeric helper can compile and simple non-contact cases can pass, but pairwise tests observe zero or stale resultant forces because only one endpoint or one matrix cell was updated.
rules.guidance: Trace every C argument of the form &array[i], &struct.field, or T *out that the callee assigns through. In Rust, write back through mutable slices and update all paired state such as previous normal force, previous tangent force, and the output vector together. For pairwise contact loops, factor a local apply_contact(src, dst) and call it once for each observable direction; do not stop after updating only the second particle or only the first particle. The completed public loop must visibly contain two update blocks per contact when both endpoints are observable: one block for `p1 -> p2` using matrix slot `p1_idx * particles_size + p2_idx` and writing `forces[p2_idx]`, and a second block for `p2 -> p1` using matrix slot `p2_idx * particles_size + p1_idx` and writing `forces[p1_idx]`. The second block is not optional just because the first block writes an equal-and-opposite force; tests may inspect each endpoint and each previous-force slot separately. Swap the normal vector sign, relative velocity order, destination properties, force matrix slot, and output force vector for the reverse block. If the available helper takes the output vector as `&Vector` or previous normal/tangent values by value, inline the arithmetic in the public loop instead of calling that helper, because those writes would be lost. Each direction must recompute with swapped particle/velocity inputs, use properties for the destination endpoint when the C code does, use its own `src * count + dst` or `dst * count + src` slot exactly as shown by C, clamp normal force and tangent friction in the same order, write the normal/tangent slots back, then add the signed normal/tangent contribution to that destination output vector. Apply global forces such as gravity after contact accumulation if the C loop does so.

rules.title: Create fixture roundtrip files relative to the test crate
rules.trigger: Tests write a file, immediately read it back, use octal-like modes, or fail with FileNotFound/Permission denied in the generated crate.
rules.goal: Make write/read roundtrips target the same project-local path and permissions.
rules.constraint: Do not use stale absolute source paths or C-style octal literals without translating their numeric value correctly. Do not create a roundtrip file with permissions that prevent the same process from reopening it for readback.
rules.risk: The production logic can be correct while generated tests fail before observing it because the file was created elsewhere or with the wrong mode.
rules.guidance: Resolve test fixture paths relative to the current output crate working directory. Ensure the write path creates parent directories as needed, truncates or replaces stale files, writes all bytes, flushes/closes before readback, and translates leading-zero C modes as octal values. If the Rust caller passes a decimal value that originated from a C octal literal, preserve the intended readable/writable owner bits defensively: create with at least 0o600, for example mode | 0o600 on Unix, rather than using the raw decimal bits as the whole permission mask.

rules.title: Keep serialized tree read/write layouts identical
rules.trigger: A tree or node hierarchy is written to a file and later read back through header bytes, node type markers, active flags, byte lengths, or recursive read_node/write_node helpers.
rules.goal: Make the writer and reader agree on one complete on-disk layout and preserve the actual root node instead of rebuilding an empty placeholder tree.
rules.constraint: Do not implement write as lossy preorder bytes or read as only header parsing when the C logic stores active datapoints, node markers, distances, and children. Do not report file-open failure merely because the translated mode lacks owner read/write bits.
rules.risk: The file can be created and compile cleanly, but readback fails or returns an empty tree because header fields, write_datapoint/read_datapoint byte order, length fields, optional markers, recursive node shape, or file permissions disagree.
rules.guidance: Define one local binary format from the C evidence before patching either side: tag plus NUL, version, branch/path/leaf parameters, datatype, padding to the header size, then recursive node records only when the read path actually consumes them. Keep header byte offsets semantic and stable: if the reader interprets the next header byte after branch/path/leaf as datatype, the writer must store the datatype there, not a root-node marker or another convenience flag. Put root/node type information in the recursive node record or another reader-matched field, not by overwriting datatype; otherwise readback can silently create a tree with the wrong element type and later inserts fail with type mismatch. Keep absolute and relative buffer offsets consistent: if the reader stores the whole file including the header in `buf`, recursive parsing can start at `HEADER_SIZE`; if it stores only bytes read after the header, recursive parsing must start at `0`. Do not read past the beginning of a post-header buffer and then return NoInternal or Unrecognized for a file the same writer just produced. Open roundtrip files with create/truncate/write and owner read/write permission at minimum; on Unix combine any caller-provided mode with `0o600` instead of using raw translated decimal bits as the whole permission mask. Flush after writing the header/body, and only then let the read path reopen the same relative path. First satisfy the local reader contract before inventing a deeper payload: if the shown reader only validates header metadata and keeps remaining bytes as an opaque buffer, write the complete header and return success rather than serializing every in-memory field. Do not make a writer fail merely because optional internal pivot/root fields, support vectors, child placeholders, or recursive helper state are absent in a simplified in-memory tree; those fields should either be omitted under a header-only reader contract or encoded with explicit absent markers that the paired reader accepts. For each optional datapoint that is actually serialized, write and read the same active marker, byte-length field, id length/string, data type or shared datatype policy, data length, data bytes, and path floats. Avoid placeholder empty nodes after readback when callers later observe the root node; reconstruct the actual root node only when the local reader consumes node records.

rules.title: Preserve existing tree contents on append
rules.trigger: A tree, index, trie, heap, or node hierarchy exposes an add/insert operation that can be called multiple times before or after a file roundtrip.
rules.goal: Make repeated inserts accumulate data instead of replacing the existing root and losing earlier entries.
rules.constraint: Do not rebuild the root from only the newly inserted batch when the tree already has a root. Do not drop existing child nodes, leaves, metrics, or stored datapoints just to simplify insertion. Do not return NoSpace merely because the simplified Rust fallback has not implemented the C split path.
rules.risk: The first insert and write can appear to work, but a second insert or readback-then-insert loses the previously written data, returns empty search results, or makes later serialization inconsistent.
rules.guidance: Handle the empty-tree case separately. When the root is absent, create the initial leaf or internal node from the new batch. When the root already exists, insert into that existing node or append to a compatible leaf and update its logical count; never translate a second add as a successful no-op. For a conservative correctness fallback, a flat leaf containing old plus new datapoints is better than replacing the root with only the new datapoints or rejecting the append. If the C split/repartition path is too large to translate locally, grow the leaf Vecs beyond leaf_capacity and keep nbpoints equal to points.len() rather than returning NoSpace; retrieval and serialization tests prefer an overfull but observable leaf to a failed second add. Preserve the tree's datatype check and allocate per-point path state for the new points, but leave existing points and root structure intact unless the C algorithm explicitly rebuilds the whole tree from both old and new data. Do not require optional pivot/support-vector fields to be present before a write can succeed if the add fallback only maintains a flat leaf; the writer should use the tree datatype/header or explicit absent markers instead of returning an argument error. After readback, an immediate add must observe a valid existing root or an intentionally empty tree, not a placeholder node that rejects insertion.

rules.title: Fix roundtrip file openability before layout
rules.trigger: A test writes a project-local file, the writer returns success, and the immediate readback fails with FileNotFound, PermissionDenied, FileOpen, or an open error.
rules.goal: Ensure the same process can reopen the same path for reading before spending repair budget on deeper serialization changes.
rules.constraint: Do not diagnose the serialized payload or invent recursive helpers while the read path cannot open the file. Do not create a file with mode bits that omit owner read permission.
rules.risk: A writer can return success after creating a write-only file, and the reader may report that as FileNotFound or FileOpen. The next repair then chases the tree or binary layout even though the first blocker is file openability.
rules.guidance: Keep the filename relative to the output crate working directory unless the C evidence requires an absolute path. In the writer, remove or truncate stale files, open with create/write/truncate, combine Unix modes defensively as `(mode as u32) | 0o600`, write all required bytes, flush, and let the handle close before readback. In the reader, map an open error to the project's file-open error consistently, but first make the writer create a readable file. Once openability is fixed, then check header offsets, byte order, and optional node records.

rules.title: Keep gap buffers fully allocated to capacity
rules.trigger: Gap-buffer text storage tracks string length, gap length, gap location, split buffers, or character lookup around the gap.
rules.goal: Maintain the C invariant that the backing storage is addressable for the whole capacity while only non-gap characters are visible.
rules.constraint: Do not create a Vec with capacity only and then index it as if its length were initialized, and do not let split/move operations expose gap bytes as text.
rules.risk: The buffer can compile and insert simple text, but empty or split lines panic with slice bounds errors because gap_len reserves capacity without allocating initialized elements.
rules.guidance: Allocate the backing buffer with actual length equal to str_len + gap_len, filling gap slots with a placeholder value. Keep gap_loc within 0..=str_len, keep gap_len + str_len equal to buffer.len(), and when moving the gap rebuild prefix, gap, middle, and suffix so all slices are in bounds. get_string and char_at should read only the prefix before gap_loc and the suffix after gap_loc + gap_len. split should move the suffix into a new fully allocated buffer with its gap at the beginning and shrink the original visible length to the prefix.

rules.title: Normalize date sentinels before calendar indexing
rules.trigger: Date parsers use C tm fields, current-time defaults, mktime-style normalization, timezone offsets, microseconds, month/day arrays, or failures from indexing with -1/usize::MAX.
rules.goal: Preserve C approximate-date behavior while keeping missing fields and overflowed calendar fields out of Rust indexes.
rules.constraint: Do not index month/day lookup tables until tm_mon is known to be in 0..12 and missing year/month/day fields have been filled or deliberately rejected.
rules.risk: A parser can handle explicit dates but panic on time-only inputs or relative forms because C sentinel -1 becomes usize::MAX, or it can drop fractional seconds while normalizing calendar fields.
rules.guidance: Treat tm_year, tm_mon, tm_mday, tm_hour, tm_min, tm_sec, and tm_usec as semantic fields first, not indexes. After scanning tokens, fill missing date fields from the reference/current time before calling tm_to_time_t or mktime-like helpers; keep parsed time and microseconds intact. If a normalization helper must handle month overflow, adjust year with div_euclid/rem_euclid so the month is 0..11 before indexing month-day tables, then normalize day underflow/overflow by moving across adjacent months. Apply timezone offsets only after constructing the timestamp, and never cast a negative sentinel to usize.

rules.title: Store hash-table payloads with wrapping hash math
rules.trigger: Open-addressed hash tables initialize capacity, compute indexes, insert payload pointers, find values, delete last-found entries, or overflow in debug hash math.
rules.goal: Preserve both key lookup and payload ownership without debug overflow panics.
rules.constraint: Do not store only keys while dropping C void* payloads, and do not use normal overflowing multiplication for hash constants that C evaluates with unsigned wrapping arithmetic.
rules.risk: A table can find the key but then panic on an empty value, or fail before lookup because debug arithmetic overflowed.
rules.guidance: Allocate owned entry storage with explicit empty/deleted markers, key fields, and payload slots. Use wrapping_add/xor/mul for C unsigned hash formulas, compute indexes with the capacity mask when capacity is a power of two, and update last-found state on successful lookup if delete depends on it.

rules.title: Preserve collection equality through comparator fallback paths
rules.trigger: Set or collection operations combine membership, contains/remove, union, intersection, difference, disjointness, custom comparators, or byte-wise default equality.
rules.goal: Make every collection operation use the same element equality semantics for insertion, lookup, removal, and derived result sets.
rules.constraint: Do not require a compare callback when the C behavior falls back to raw byte equality, do not transmute a value into a wider destination, and do not drop the comparator when constructing union/intersection/difference results.
rules.risk: A collection can build successfully but later panic on a missing compare function, misclassify membership, or make derived sets disagree with contains/remove.
rules.guidance: Centralize equality in a local helper: use the supplied comparator when present; otherwise compare exactly the stored element width, using typed equality when available or safe byte-slice equality over size_of::<T>(). Carry the comparator and element width into result collections produced by union, intersection, difference, clone, or copy operations. Prefer callable-only fixes; if the only viable repair target is a whole impl block, preserve every existing public method that tests or callers can name, because cargo check can pass while integration tests fail to compile after a partial impl replacement. If a helper is defined inside the same generic impl, call it as Self::helper without adding an unnecessary turbofish; if hashing bytes locally, either use already-imported traits or avoid trait-dependent hasher methods in the patch. Avoid transmute_copy between differently sized types; copy only the bytes or typed value actually stored.

rules.title: Initialize open-address buckets with the probed empty sentinel
rules.trigger: An open-addressed set or map times out in insertion, probes bucket slots, and uses a signed marker field such as a probe index or distance to distinguish empty, occupied, and deleted slots.
rules.goal: Make the first insertion and every resize observe real empty buckets with the same sentinel that lookup/removal/probing tests use.
rules.constraint: Do not zero-initialize buckets when the probing loop treats a negative marker as empty; do not use capacity as the logical element count.
rules.risk: A table can compile and even expose the expected capacity, but the first insert loops forever because every zeroed bucket looks occupied.
rules.guidance: Define one bucket-state convention before implementing add/contains/remove: for example, empty/deleted when the marker field is negative and occupied when it is nonnegative. Allocate initial and resized bucket arrays by constructing explicit empty bucket values with that negative marker, then keep a separate logical size that increments only on new inserts and decrements only on successful removals. Every probing loop should either find that sentinel or stop after one full table scan and grow/rebuild instead of looping forever.

rules.title: Keep open-addressed set probing and equality state together
rules.trigger: An open-addressed set or map exposes add/remove/contains/iteration plus load factors, resize, hash callbacks, byte comparators, or bucket probe indexes.
rules.goal: Make membership operations, resizing, and derived set operations observe the same bucket state, probe sequence, and equality semantics.
rules.constraint: Do not replace C hash callbacks or double-hash probing with DefaultHasher plus simple linear probing when the C evidence has explicit hash1/hash2, seed, probe index, or load-factor resize state. Do not add Hash, Eq, PartialEq, Clone, or Copy bounds to generic public methods or impls unless those bounds are already present in the shown signature. Do not store an arbitrary signed cast of a hash in the occupancy marker when negative marker values mean empty or deleted. Do not panic, return empty, leave `unimplemented!()`, or skip membership work when the compare callback is absent if the C behavior falls back to byte equality.
rules.risk: The table may compile but most membership tests fail or hang because inserts land in different buckets than lookups, resize drops the old probe state, iteration drains the table, derived result buckets contain no empty sentinel, or default byte equality is treated as an error.
rules.guidance: Define one local equality helper and one local insertion path, then use them for add, remove, contains, iteration-backed operations, union, intersection, difference, disjointness, and resize. Keep every public method signature exactly as shown: for `impl<T>` methods, do not add `where T: Hash`, `T: PartialEq`, `T: Eq`, `T: Clone`, or `T: Copy` to make the code compile. Hash unconstrained generic values from their raw bytes with the shown C hash callback or a local byte hasher; equality must be total: call the custom comparator when present and otherwise compare exactly the stored element bytes with size_of::<T>(), not `PartialEq`. If helper logic is kept inside one callable, write valid Rust nested helpers: `fn helper<T>(...) -> ... { ... }` for named functions or `let helper = |...| -> ... { ... };` for closures. Never emit C-style pseudo declarations such as `helper(arg: Type) -> Ret { ... }` without the `fn` keyword. Avoid recursive closures for insertion/growth paths; use a nested `fn` with every needed state passed as parameters, or use an explicit loop/rebuild path. Use one identical hash/probe formula for insert, lookup, remove, and resize. Do not write separate simplified hash functions in add/remove/contains, do not change the secondary step formula between methods, and do not make contains/remove use a different seed or constants than add. For power-of-two bucket capacities, the secondary probe step must be coprime to capacity; use an odd nonzero step such as `(hash2 | 1) % capacity` with zero mapped to 1, not `hash2 % (capacity - 1) + 1` which can be even and cycle through only part of the table. If shared helpers cannot be added and keeping the probe formula identical is risky, implement contains/remove/derived membership by scanning occupied buckets with the same equality helper; a bounded O(n) scan is preferable to a mismatched probe that misses inserted elements, and scanning occupied buckets should be the default safe fallback for public set semantics. Initialize public sets with the C initial capacity and explicit empty buckets when capacity/init tests expect that shape; do not make `new()` or `init()` an empty Vec with capacity 0 unless the C API also reports zero capacity. For empty bucket arrays and resized arrays, do not use `vec![sentinel; n]` or `sentinel.clone()` unless Clone is already available; instead push a freshly constructed empty bucket for each slot, preserving the negative marker. Keep logical size separate from bucket capacity: size counts occupied elements, capacity counts slots, and loops over elements should scan occupied buckets rather than calling a by-index accessor with 0..size unless indexes are known to be dense. If the shared field name looks like bucket_size but capacity/init tests expect it to equal the number of allocated buckets, treat that field as capacity and compute logical size by counting occupied buckets or by a separate counter; do not repurpose the capacity field as the live element count. Preserve the bucket marker convention: negative or dedicated markers for empty/deleted, occupied markers for live slots. If the marker field is signed and negative values are empty/deleted, do not write `hash as i32` or any truncated hash into it; use a known nonnegative occupancy/probe marker such as the probe distance or 1, and store the full hash only in a separate field when one exists. After a successful new insert, the next size/count observation must increase exactly once; after a duplicate insert it must not change. Every probing loop in add, remove, and contains must be bounded by at most one full table scan; never write an unbounded `loop` that stops only on an empty sentinel, because derived or full tables can temporarily have no empty slots. If an add scans the whole table without finding a slot, do not recursively call add again at the same capacity; grow or rebuild into fresh empty buckets and retry with an iterative loop or return a real failure according to the C API. On resize or derived-set construction, rebuild every occupied element into freshly initialized empty buckets and update logical size separately from capacity. Derived result sets must not be represented as a dense vector containing only occupied buckets; allocate extra empty sentinel slots or insert each result element through the same add/equality path so later contains/remove calls can terminate on misses. A derived operation that writes directly into the first empty result bucket must first ensure the result has enough spare slots for all possible matches and must grow/rebuild before the slot scan is exhausted; never panic or return a dummy failure just because a reused result set previously had a smaller capacity. Reusing a result set for a larger union/intersection/difference must clear old markers, preserve configuration, then grow or call the common add path for each survivor so the new logical size can exceed the previous result size. If the public API only requires set semantics and not stable bucket positions, a simple coherent scan-plus-add rebuild is safer than mixing hash probes, copied probe indexes, and direct bucket placement. Iteration over occupied buckets should observe elements without clearing bucket markers, replacing buckets, taking ownership of the whole bucket vector, or decrementing logical size unless the C API explicitly consumes the set; for by-value iteration over C-like plain data, use a narrow pointer read of each occupied element and leave the bucket state unchanged, and a following contains/size call must still observe the same set. Derived sets must carry the comparator, element width, seed, load factors, and sentinel policy, and should insert through the same add/equality path to avoid duplicates. A compile fallback that leaves `unimplemented!()`, `todo!()`, `panic!()`, or a dummy success return in add/remove/contains/iter/union/intersection/difference/clear is not an implementation; repair the shared helper or callable instead.

rules.title: Copy bucket values without adding Clone bounds
rules.trigger: A bucket or vector accessor returns a stored generic element by value and compile repair reports a move from an index or a missing clone method.
rules.goal: Preserve C value-copy accessor semantics without changing the public generic bounds.
rules.constraint: Do not add Clone or Copy bounds to a public impl just to satisfy one accessor, and do not call clone when the stored element type is unconstrained.
rules.risk: A direct Rust move from an indexed bucket fails to compile; a clone-based repair also fails or changes the interface contract by requiring Clone.
rules.guidance: For an accessor whose C macro returns the stored element value from an occupied bucket, emulate the C by-value copy at that boundary with a narrow unsafe pointer read from the element slot. Keep the occupancy marker and bucket array unchanged, and use this only for by-value accessors, not for observing iterators that must leave elements owned in place.
keywords: does not implement the Copy trait

rules.title: Return mutable field accessors from shared receivers with raw field addresses
rules.trigger: A fixed public accessor signature returns a mutable reference from a shared receiver and compile repair reports invalid reference casting or borrowing behind a shared reference.
rules.goal: Keep the required interface while avoiding linted casts through an intermediate shared reference.
rules.constraint: Do not change the public receiver from shared to mutable, and do not cast `&field` to `&mut field` through a shared reference.
rules.risk: A direct borrow cannot compile, and a repair that casts `&field as *const _ as *mut _` is rejected by invalid-reference-casting lints.
rules.guidance: When the interface is fixed as shared receiver to mutable field reference, take the raw field address directly with core::ptr::addr_of!(self.field), cast that raw pointer to mut, and dereference it in one narrow unsafe block. Apply this only to accessor shims whose caller-visible contract already requires mutable access from a shared receiver; otherwise prefer a normal mutable receiver.

rules.title: Store sparse bitmap groups by rank, not dense index offsets
rules.trigger: A sparse array or sparse dictionary stores elements in bitmap-marked groups and computes get/set positions from group bit counts.
rules.goal: Preserve compact sparse storage and dictionary ownership while making absent keys and overwritten values observable.
rules.constraint: Do not store elements at `index * elem_size` inside a sparse group when the C code packs only occupied slots, and do not accept, truncate, or pad an inserted value whose byte length is larger than the configured element size when the C API reports failure. Do not keep raw pointers to temporary key/value buffers for dictionary buckets. Do not serialize, memcpy, shift, or drop Rust-owned dictionary buckets (`String`, `Vec`, `Box`, raw allocation pointers, or pointer/length pairs) as anonymous bytes inside a `Vec<u8>` sparse group. Do not invent a bucket owner type that disagrees with the shared bucket struct fields already shown in the prompt.
rules.risk: Basic set calls may appear to work, but get returns the wrong slot or dangling data once keys collide, many keys are inserted, an earlier sparse index is absent, value sizes differ, or resizing copies pointer-owning bucket bytes and corrupts the heap. A repair can also fail compilation if it stores Vec<u8> into a String key field, wraps buckets in Box when callers expect plain values, or calls a helper that was not actually defined.
rules.guidance: For each group, use the occupancy bitmap to compute rank: count set bits before the target position. Reject out-of-range indexes and reject values larger than the group's fixed element size before mutating the bitmap; only shorter values may be zero-padded when the C code does so. On insert, set the bit, grow the compact byte storage by exactly one fixed-size element, shift later occupied elements right, and write the new element at `rank * elem_size`; on overwrite, write in place at that rank without changing the slot width. On get, return None when the bit is clear and otherwise read the compact rank slot. Keep the generic sparse-array byte storage for plain fixed-width byte elements only. For dictionary buckets, store typed owned key and value bytes together with hash and lengths in a durable owner such as `Option<Bucket>`, `Vec<Option<Bucket>>`, or another dict-owned table; do not represent a bucket as raw bytes containing pointers, and do not reconstruct `Vec::from_raw_parts` from copied pointer fields. Match the shown shared item exactly: if the bucket key field is `String`, store a valid `String` derived from the key bytes or change every affected shared item and call site consistently; if the table field is `Vec<Option<Bucket>>`, do not return `Vec<Option<Box<Bucket>>>` unless all signatures and field types are patched together. If a resize helper is needed, define it in the same callable as a valid nested `fn` or patch a real shared helper; do not call an imagined `rehash`, `grow`, or `resize` helper by name. If a compact sparse index is still useful for the dictionary, let it point to or index typed owned buckets rather than owning their raw memory image. If a byte serialization is unavoidable, define one self-describing layout and use that exact layout in both set and get; do not write `[key length, key, value length, value, hash]` in one path and read `[hash, key length, key, value length, value]` in another. Do not change a sparse group's `elem_size` to each bucket's serialized length or mix variable-length records with the generic rank calculation; use a separate length-prefixed dictionary slot store or a typed owner for variable-sized values. Probing should compare key bytes and lengths before overwriting or reporting a hit. Probe until an empty slot is found or one full table scan completes; do not stop after `bucket_count` probes, because collisions can require more probes than the number of live entries before reaching the first empty bucket. After a successful new insert, increment the live bucket count exactly once; after replacing an existing key, leave it unchanged. When load reaches the resize threshold, actually allocate the larger bucket array and reinsert every occupied typed bucket through the same hash/probe path, moving owned key/value objects exactly once; do not byte-copy ownership records and do not leave a comment saying resize is omitted while still returning success.

rules.title: Use block ECC syndrome parity instead of byte XOR checksums
rules.trigger: Block error-correcting code encoders or decoders add parity bytes, correct one-bit errors, reject double-bit errors, or process fixed-size data blocks.
rules.goal: Preserve the C block-level ECC syndrome behavior for encoding and decoding rather than a checksum-only approximation.
rules.constraint: Do not implement the parity byte as a simple XOR checksum of the data bytes, and do not decode by blindly dropping every parity byte when tests or C code exercise single-bit correction and double-bit detection.
rules.risk: The output length can be right while parity bytes, corrected data, and double-error rejection are wrong.
rules.guidance: Model each fixed-size data block as individual bits plus a parity/syndrome byte. If the public encode/decode wrapper calls a helper named like an ECC/Hamming encode_impl or decode_impl and the helper body is not shown, inline the helper semantics instead of replacing it with a byte XOR checksum. Encoding should compute the same syndrome/parity bit positions as the C implementation over the block, append the block parity byte, and handle partial trailing blocks with the same reduced data length. Decoding should recompute syndrome, correct the addressed single-bit data error when the syndrome identifies one, accept clean blocks, and reject uncorrectable double-bit errors rather than returning corrupted data. Keep output sizing separate from correction logic.

rules.title: Decode Hamming blocks from position syndrome plus overall parity
rules.trigger: A Hamming-style block encoder stores one check byte whose low bits are an xor of logical bit positions and whose high bit stores overall parity.
rules.goal: Correct exactly one data-bit error and reject double-bit errors using the same syndrome/parity decision tree as the C implementation.
rules.constraint: Do not brute-force every possible bit flip until parity matches, do not treat a parity-bit error as a data-byte correction, and do not special-case literal test input/output byte arrays or one observed fixture.
rules.risk: Brute-force correction or fixture-specific branches can silently turn double-bit errors into plausible data, flip the wrong data bit while still matching the parity byte, or pass one encode assertion while failing roundtrip and error-correction tests.
rules.guidance: Use one shared data-bit to Hamming-position mapping for both encode and decode. Walk data bits in byte/bit order while incrementing a logical position counter and skipping Hamming parity positions 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and so on before assigning each data bit its position. Encoding should xor those non-power-of-two positions for set data bits into the low seven syndrome bits, compute overall parity across data bits plus the low syndrome bits, and store the high check bit according to the C odd/even parity convention. Decoding should recompute the same position xor from the received data, xor it with `check & 0x7f`, and decide from that syndrome plus overall parity. If syndrome is zero, copy data unchanged. If syndrome is nonzero but overall parity says there were at least two errors, reject the block. If syndrome is a power of two, only a parity position is wrong, so leave data unchanged and accept. Otherwise map the non-power-of-two syndrome back to a data bit with `data_bit = syndrome - floor_log2(syndrome) - 2`, then flip only that addressed data bit when it lies inside the block. A byte-wise xor checksum or hard-coded known vector is never this algorithm, even if the wrapper helper body is not included in the prompt.

rules.title: Read compact random key tables through one bounds-safe helper
rules.trigger: A hash or polynomial multiply routine indexes a fixed random/key table using large byte offsets, key offsets, polynomial offsets, final-key offsets, or per-block key indexes.
rules.goal: Keep key-dependent hashing deterministic without panicking when the public key slice is compact or shorter than C's internal expanded table.
rules.constraint: Do not read key material with direct slice ranges such as `random[key_offset..key_offset + 8]`, `random[poly_offset..]`, or `words[index]` unless that exact range was proven in bounds for every input length. Do not return 0, `(0, 0)`, or a dummy constant when a polynomial/final/length key window is outside the public key slice. Do not turn the C internal expanded-table size into a Rust public precondition such as `assert!(random.len() >= RANDOM_BYTES_NEEDED...)`.
rules.risk: A hash can pass the example that uses a generated full key but panic on unit, avalanche, collision, or short-key tests with a custom compact key slice before hashing semantics are observed. If missing high key words are zero-filled, fixed byte offsets are read directly from a compact slice, or compact key bytes are folded into one u64 with shifts such as `byte << (8 * i)` for i greater than seven, short-key tests can panic, collapse every hash to 0, or make different late-block inputs hash identically.
rules.guidance: Create one local helper for all random/key reads, for example `key_word(index) -> u64`, before deriving polynomial, final, length, or per-block keys. The helper must be safe and non-degenerate for every index: read available little-endian bytes when present; when the requested word is outside the compact slice, derive a deterministic nonzero word from the compact seed bytes and the requested index by wrapping through available words and mixing with splitmix-style constants, rotations, and the index. If folding all compact key bytes into a u64 seed, either process eight-byte chunks, rotate/xor each byte, or shift by `(8 * (i % 8))`; never shift a u64 byte by `8 * i` when i can be 8 or larger. Do not zero-fill any missing key word, do not return 0 for out-of-range key reads, and do not use a formula such as `seed * index + index` that returns 0 for missing word 0. If only one or two u64 seed words are available, synthesize distinct key words for all later per-block, tail, polynomial, final, adjacent, and length-key indexes from those seed words; otherwise long messages can ignore later bytes and avalanche or distinct-input checks collapse. Use this helper for per-block keys, tail keys, polynomial keys, final keys, key-length words, adjacent key pairs, top-level functions, and hasher-stored keys. Fixed internal offsets such as polynomial/final/length keys are key indexes too: derive them from word indexes, not direct byte offsets into the compact public slice. For example, a fixed byte offset equal to `N * 8` names `key_word(N)`, not a direct slice read at byte `N * 8`; never special-case those offsets with direct fixed-window reads or `(0, 0)`/`0` fallbacks. If a generated loop tracks message progress in 64-bit words, convert to bytes before reading the message: byte offset is `word_index * 8`. Do not mix word counts and byte offsets in long-block paths, because a loop variable that has advanced by words but is passed directly to a byte-reader can re-read early bytes and ignore later blocks. For every full-block and remainder path, each message word after the first block must be paired with a distinct derived adjacent key word and folded into the accumulator; late-block or tail differences must not be invisible. If the public function accepts `random: &[u8]` or similar key material, accept any nonempty compact slice and make even empty slices deterministic instead of asserting an internal SIMD/precomputed table length. Do not leave any direct `random[...]`, `random[a..b]`, `keys[...]`, `words[index]`, generated-table length assert, expanded-vector indexing path, `try_into().unwrap()` on a fixed key window, or out-of-range zero fallback beside the helper, including in top-level byte-slice hash functions.
keywords: random buffer must be at least

rules.title: Turn 64-bit limb shifts into cross-limb carries
rules.trigger: Carry-less multiplication combines 64x64 partial products into 128-bit or 256-bit low/high limbs.
rules.goal: Compile wide carry-less arithmetic without losing the contribution of cross terms.
rules.constraint: Never write `u64 << 64`, `u64 >> 64`, `u128 << 128`, or `u128 >> 128`; these whole-limb shifts are moves between low/high variables, not Rust shift expressions. Do not replace them with `wrapping_shr(64)` or `wrapping_shl(64)`. Do not implement carry-less multiply with ordinary integer multiplication, including `(a as u128) * (b as u128)`, `wrapping_mul`, or add/carry arithmetic.
rules.risk: The code can fail to compile with arithmetic overflow even though the intended C/SIMD operation is just placing a partial product in the next limb. Using wrapping shifts can compile but make the high limb equal the low limb when the shift count is zero, causing XOR reductions to collapse hashes to 0.
rules.guidance: When a 64x64 carry-less product returns `(lo, hi)`, combining `(p01 << 64)` means `p01.lo` contributes to the high 64-bit limb and contributes zero to the low 64-bit limb; `p01.hi` contributes to the next higher limb. Implement scalar carry-less multiply by scanning set bits and XORing shifted multiplicand contributions into explicit low/high limbs; every contribution combines with XOR, never integer `*`, addition, or carries. If a source value is already only a u64 or usize and the C expression asks for its high 64-bit half, that half is the literal value 0; never write `(value as u64) >> 64`, `value.wrapping_shr(64)`, or an equivalent expression even when it feeds a tuple high limb. In a scalar `for i in 0..64` carry-less multiply, the low contribution is `a << i`, and the high contribution is `0` when `i == 0`, otherwise `a >> (64 - i)`; never compute the `i == 0` case as `a.wrapping_shr(64)`. For a low 128-bit result, use two u64 limbs: `low_lo = p00_lo` and `low_hi = p00_hi ^ p01_lo ^ p10_lo`; do not write `p01_lo << 64`, `p10_lo << 64`, `p01_lo >> 64`, or `p10_lo >> 64` in code or comments. For the full 256-bit product, keep four u64 limbs such as `z0 = p00_lo`, `z1 = p00_hi ^ p01_lo ^ p10_lo`, `z2 = p01_hi ^ p10_hi ^ p11_lo`, and `z3 = p11_hi`; do not collapse those limbs into a u128 and then shift that u128 by 64 to recover halves. Terms shifted by exactly the full result width, such as `p11 << 128` for the low 128 bits, contribute zero to that low result. For generic multi-limb shifts by `s`, split `word_shift = s / 64` and `bit_shift = s % 64`; when `bit_shift == 0`, move whole limbs only and do not compute `src >> (64 - bit_shift)` or `src << (64 - bit_shift)`.

rules.title: Resolve generated test helper binaries in the output crate
rules.trigger: Generated tests spawn build-relative parser/checker/helper binaries that are absent from the translated Rust crate.
rules.goal: Run the available project-local binary instead of failing before semantic assertions.
rules.constraint: Do not leave Command::new on a missing build/ path when an equivalent src/bin or Cargo target binary exists.
rules.risk: A semantic improvement is invisible if tests fail at process spawn with No such file.
rules.guidance: Map build-relative helper commands to the current executable directory, Cargo target debug binaries, or generated src/bin names. Keep arguments and expected stdout/stderr semantics unchanged.

rules.title: Expand definition nodes by mutating the observed tree
rules.trigger: Expression reducers, definition tables, AST nodes, or type/equality checks expect a definition variable to become the table entry.
rules.goal: Replace definition nodes with semantic copies and compare expression types by meaning, not pointer identity.
rules.constraint: Do not compute an expanded replacement and then drop it without mutating the caller-visible AST node, even when the fixed Rust signature exposes the node through a shared reference.
rules.risk: A reducer can parse and type most expressions but still fail when definition expansion leaves the observed node unchanged, or when a public signature copied from C hides mutation behind an immutable Rust reference.
rules.guidance: When a node references a definition table entry, deep-copy or reconstruct the table entry into the observed node, then recursively expand inside applications and abstractions. If the public signature is fixed as `&AstNode` but tests or C semantics pass a mutable node expecting in-place expansion, use one narrow raw-pointer cast at the entrypoint to write the replacement, then keep recursive helpers normally mutable. Do not leave comments saying expansion happens elsewhere. For type equality, compare the expression's type structure or canonical type string rather than unrelated pointer identity.

rules.title: Generate alpha-conversion names with a monotonic counter
rules.trigger: Lambda-calculus or AST parser code alpha-converts variables, checks used names, or needs fresh variable names during substitution or lambda parsing.
rules.goal: Return deterministic fresh names that match the C counter semantics and avoid variable capture.
rules.constraint: Do not use a constant suffix such as `_fresh` for every variable, and do not reset the fresh counter on each call.
rules.risk: The parser can create lambdas and substitute terms but still fail alpha-conversion tests or capture variables because every fresh name collides or has the wrong numeric suffix.
rules.guidance: Keep one process-local monotonically increasing counter for alpha conversion. Each call should append the next numeric suffix to the original variable name, for example `name_1`, `name_2`, and so on, while preserving the original base name. Use atomic or mutex state if a plain static mutable counter would be unsafe, and keep the counter shared across parser calls rather than local to one function invocation.

rules.title: Rebuild proof roots from the indexed leaf subset
rules.trigger: A proof verifier receives all leaves plus proof indices, sibling lemmas, or tree-node positions for only the proven leaves.
rules.goal: Reconstruct the proof root from the leaves named by the proof indices instead of pairing proof indices with every input leaf in order or passing a full leaf list to a subset-only root helper.
rules.constraint: In verifier functions, the first validation should only reject empty proof indices or empty leaves; do not write `if leaves.len() != proof.indices.len()` or equivalent when proof indices identify a subset of a larger leaf list, even if a generated comment claims that this is the C logic. Do not call a proof-root helper with full leaves if that helper checks leaves.len() == proof.indices.len(), and do not sort the full leaves array and zip its first elements with proof indices. Do not allocate, queue, or validate one initial pair per full leaf when the proof has fewer indices; proof-root capacity and initial queue length must be based on the proof-indexed subset count. Do not treat absolute tree-node proof indices as zero-based positions into the full leaf array.
rules.risk: A verifier can build proofs correctly but reject a valid subset proof because it returns an error on full_leaves.len() != proof.indices.len(), calls the root-rebuild helper with the wrong full-leaf argument, pairs proof indices with the wrong leaves after sorting all leaves independently, or uses the wrong sibling parity while rebuilding parents.
rules.guidance: Treat the verifier leaves argument as the full leaf set unless the local Rust contract proves otherwise. At the verifier boundary, first reject only empty proof indices or empty full leaves. Then derive the leaf offset from the full leaf count, usually `leaf_offset = full_leaves.len() - 1` for a zero-based array heap, map each absolute proof tree index back to its original leaf position with `leaf_pos = index - leaf_offset`, reject only indices that map outside the full leaf range, collect only those indexed leaves, and keep each collected leaf paired with its own proof index before root reconstruction. A verifier or proof-root helper that begins by comparing full_leaves.len() with proof.indices.len() is wrong for subset proofs; delete that guard rather than preserving it in a duplicated local helper. If the proof-root helper is called from a verifier with the full leaf set, it must either collect the proof-indexed subset internally before validating lengths or the verifier must pass that subset; never leave an early `leaves.nodes.len() != proof.indices.values.len()` return on that path. A verifier that sorts every full leaf by node bytes and pairs the first sorted leaves with proof indices is also wrong; only the proof-indexed subset participates in the proof queue. If an existing proof-root helper expects one leaf per proof index, pass this subset to it; otherwise rebuild directly in the verifier from the subset pairs. If both `proof_root` and `proof_verify` are implemented, both must use the same subset mapping; fixing only one while the other keeps the full-leaves equality guard still rejects valid subset proofs. In the subset rebuild path, capacity checks, temporary buffer sizes, queue initialization, loop bounds, `for i in ...` ranges, and copied pair buffers should use `proof.indices.len()` or the collected subset length, not the full leaf count. Never loop over `0..full_leaves.len()` while indexing `proof.indices[i]`, and never clone/sort all full leaves before zipping with proof indices, because subset proofs have fewer proof indices than full leaves. It is valid for a proof over fewer leaves to be checked against a larger full leaf list. Rebuild upward with queued node/index pairs and consume lemmas only for missing siblings. For zero-based binary heap indices, children of parent `p` are `2*p + 1` on the left and `2*p + 2` on the right, so an odd index is a left child whose sibling is `index + 1`, an even nonzero index is a right child whose sibling is `index - 1`, and the parent is `(index - 1) >> 1`; the compact formula `((index + 1) ^ 1) - 1` is a safe sibling expression for nonzero indices. Preserve left/right merge order from that parity: odd current node merges as `(current, sibling)`, even current node merges as `(sibling, current)`. Sort queue pairs by tree index when the C code does so, and accept success only when the computed index reaches the root and all lemmas are consumed. When queue entries are structs containing nodes, move them with pop/remove or rebuild fields explicitly; do not use `.copied()` or require the pair type to implement Copy.

rules.title: Keep range Feistel halves bounded with modular arithmetic
rules.trigger: A format-preserving or range-limited Feistel permutation uses sqrt-sized halves, round keys, or a block cipher round function.
rules.goal: Keep encrypt/decrypt as inverse permutations inside the bounded range without debug overflow panics.
rules.constraint: Do not combine Feistel halves with unbounded XOR output when the C logic reduces each round function modulo the half range. Do not leave private helpers called by public encrypt/decrypt paths with `unimplemented!()`, `todo!()`, `panic!("not implemented")`, or dummy constants just because the public methods inline one copy of the logic.
rules.risk: The permutation can compile and work for small examples, then panic on `left * base + right` overflow or fail decrypt(encrypt(x)) when the round output is not reduced. A public method that calls an unimplemented private `fe`, `fe_inv`, `f`, or key-expansion helper can pass translation but panic before semantic assertions run; using normal `+` in unsigned Speck/key-schedule arithmetic can panic in debug builds.
rules.guidance: Compute left/right halves with division and modulo by the square-root base, then keep both halves below that base after every round. Implement every helper reachable from public encrypt/decrypt/new paths, including Feistel round, inverse round, key expansion, and block round helpers; if public methods call `self.fe`, `self.fe_inv`, `self.f`, or a key-schedule function, those helpers must contain the real logic rather than placeholders. If the current repair is limited to one public callable and a reachable private helper is shown as a stub, inline the complete helper chain as local functions or closures inside that public callable instead of calling the stub. Do this for every public path independently: a decrypt method that inlines the round logic does not make an encrypt method safe if encrypt still calls an unfinished helper. Implement one forward round function from the expanded round keys and call that same function from both encryption and decryption; the inverse Feistel network does not decrypt the round function itself. Preserve the local helper argument order from the C/Rust signature: if a function like `f(j, r)` uses `r` to select the key row and `j` as the half-block input, call it as `f(half, round)`, not `f(round, half)`. In forward rounds, rotate halves as `new_left = right` and `new_right = (left + f(right, round)) % base` when the C code uses modular addition; do not substitute XOR unless the source does. In inverse rounds over reversed round indexes, evaluate the same round function on the current left half and recover the previous left with `(right + base - (f % base)) % base`, then set the previous right to the current left. Recombine in the same half order used by the split, for example `right * base + left` when splitting used `left = m % base` and `right = m / base`; do this only after both halves are bounded below the base. For Speck-style 32-bit word rounds and key expansion, use wrapping_add plus rotations and XOR exactly as the C variant specifies; do not use normal `+`, and do not default to 7/2 rotations when the shown C code uses 8/3 rotations or xors the round counter into the key schedule. Cycle-walk out-of-range ciphertexts by repeatedly applying the same full forward or inverse permutation.

rules.title: Build wide carry-less products from explicit limbs
rules.trigger: Carry-less multiply, SIMD-style 128-bit vectors, polynomial hash reduction, lazy modulo, high/low product halves, compact public key/random fixtures, or wide shift diagnostics appear.
rules.goal: Avoid invalid word-size or wider shifts while preserving the needed low and high product limbs and caller-visible key behavior.
rules.constraint: Never shift a Rust u128 by 128 bits or a Rust u64 by 64 bits, do not model a 256-bit product as a single u128, do not replace carry-less polynomial hashing with ordinary wrapping_mul/add mixing, do not implement a helper named like `clmul` with `(a as u128) * (b as u128)` or any ordinary integer multiply, do not leave any public hash entrypoint, long-message branch, short-message branch, hasher method, or helper with `unimplemented!()`, `todo!()`, `panic!()`, placeholder comments, or a dummy constant return, do not use normal Rust `+` or `*` in unsigned key/random expansion state updates, and do not reject, assert, or panic on a shorter public key/random slice unless the Rust interface signature itself requires an expanded buffer.
rules.risk: Placeholder wide arithmetic such as product >> 128 fails compilation and can distract repair toward unrelated SIMD imports; a half-written top-level hash or long-message branch that ends in `unimplemented!()`, `todo!()`, `panic!()`, `unreachable!()`, or a comment saying the branch is not needed for tests can compile but panic when longer public inputs are exercised; enforcing a C-internal precomputed-key byte count can make public tests panic before hashing semantics are observed; ordinary integer hash mixing can pass simple inequality checks while breaking GF(2) xor-difference invariants; compact expanded-key vectors can pass short inputs but panic on long inputs when an adjacent key index equals the vector length; a generated key helper can panic in debug builds if unsigned PRNG output uses normal `state0 + state1`; direct eight-byte reads from message tails or compact keys can panic on short strings; zero-filled missing keys, word-count variables used as byte offsets, a scalar carry-less multiply that xors shifted carry bits into the high limb even when the multiplier bit is clear, XORing the same tail word into both limbs, symmetric `(x, x)` length mixing followed by `lo ^ hi`, or reading final keys and then not using them can collapse changed inputs to identical short or long hashes; an unbounded bit-by-bit polynomial reduction inside the hash hot path can pass early avalanche checks but time out on collision loops.
rules.guidance: Carry-less multiply two u64 values into u128, split 128-bit inputs into low/high u64 limbs, and combine partial products into explicit low/high halves. A scalar `clmul` helper must iterate over the bit index or over set bits of one operand and XOR the shifted multiplicand into the result only when that multiplier bit is set; do not mutate a shifted multiplicand and XOR each left-shift carry into the high limb on every loop iteration independent of the multiplier bit. Ordinary integer multiplication such as `(a as u128) * (b as u128)`, `wrapping_mul`, addition, or carry propagation is a different arithmetic and breaks GF(2) linearity. For shifts by an entire limb width, move/swap limbs directly instead of writing << 64, >> 64, << 128, or >> 128. In scalar carry-less multiplication, handle the zero-shift case explicitly: for bit index 0 the high-limb contribution is 0, not `a.wrapping_shr(64)`. For bit index `i > 0`, the high contribution is `a >> (64 - i)` and must be XORed only for a set multiplier bit at `i`; the low contribution should use `a.wrapping_shl(i as u32)` or an explicit branch, not `a << i` with a runtime shift count. For generic multi-limb polynomial reduction shifts, branch on `bit_shift = shift % 64`; if it is zero, copy whole limbs to the shifted positions and skip all cross-limb `>> (64 - bit_shift)` terms. If a shifted temporary is still typed as u64, its high 64-bit half is literally 0: code like `let ml = mlo << shift; z1 ^= ml >> 64` is always invalid and must be replaced either by `0` for the high half or by computing a u128 temporary such as `let wide = (mlo as u128) << shift; low = wide as u64; high = (wide >> 64) as u64`. For cross-limb contributions without u128, use `if shift == 0 { 0 } else { mlo >> (64 - shift) }`, never `mlo >> 64`. When multiplying two 128-bit values from 64-bit halves, compute four explicit u64 product limbs: `z0 = p00_lo`, `z1 = p00_hi ^ p01_lo ^ p10_lo`, `z2 = p01_hi ^ p10_hi ^ p11_lo`, `z3 = p11_hi`. The low 128 bits are `(z0, z1)` and the high 128 bits are `(z2, z3)`; never spell this as `(p01_lo << 64)`, `(p10_lo << 64)`, `(p01_lo >> 64)`, `(p10_lo >> 64)`, `(p01_hi << 64)`, `(p10_hi << 64)`, or `high >> 64`, even in comments that the repair model may copy. When accumulating the low 128 bits, any partial product shifted by 128 or more contributes zero to that low half; when accumulating the high half, move the appropriate unshifted or limb-shifted partial into the high accumulator instead of spelling a 128-bit shift. In formulas such as `p00 ^ (p10 << 64) ^ (p20 << 64) ^ (p30 << 128)`, do not emit the final `<< 128` term in Rust; split the expression into low/high halves first. If a value is only u64 and the C expression wants its high 64-bit half, use 0 directly; never write value >> 64, even if the result is later masked away. For C unsigned key generation, seed expansion, random table generation, or xorshift-style state updates, every state addition, multiplication, and left shift that can overflow must use wrapping operations; the output word from adding two unsigned state words must be `wrapping_add`, not normal `+`, even when the helper only prepares keys for the hash. When C internals mention a large aligned random/key table but the Rust callable accepts an arbitrary byte slice, treat the slice as compact public key material. Put all reads behind one `key_word(index)` helper that is bounds-safe and non-degenerate for every possible index: if `index * 8 + byte` is outside the slice, derive a deterministic nonzero word from the compact slice and index rather than returning 0 for all missing words. Use this helper for per-block keys, tail keys, polynomial keys, final keys, key-length words, adjacent key pairs, and stored hasher key material. Put message reads behind a separate bounds-safe little-endian helper too: build each word byte-by-byte from the available input bytes, zero-pad only the missing tail bytes, and never read `slice[offset..offset + 8]` unless `offset + 8 <= slice.len()`. Keep message positions typed by unit: a word counter is not a byte offset, so read word `w` at byte offset `w * 8`; a byte offset should not be multiplied again. In long-message loops, advance by the number of 64-bit words consumed, then convert to bytes only at the read boundary. For each full block, each pair of words must use an adjacent derived key pair that depends on the block-local pair index and block number; for a partial remainder, read exactly the remaining words and tail bytes, use the matching derived key pair, and include the length. For partial final words, derive the tail from the actual remaining bytes, mix it with the corresponding derived key exactly once, and include the message length. Never include the same partial tail as both an already zero-padded message word and a separate extra word. Never write `random[offset]`, `random[offset + 7]`, `string[offset + 7]`, `slice[offset..offset + 8]`, or `words[index]` unless a bounds check or helper has first made the access safe; fixed internal key offsets must be converted to key-word indexes and routed through the helper rather than zero-filled byte reads. Translate every public hash entrypoint through to a real return value for every length, including empty, sub-word, short, multi-block, and long messages: build the scalar half-product, tail-word, polynomial reduction, length-mixing, and final reduction path locally when the C/SIMD helpers are unavailable, and remove every placeholder branch before returning. If the module has both a top-level byte-slice hash callable and a hasher method, implement one shared complete hashing path or make one delegate to the other; do not leave the top-level callable with a separate simplified short-only implementation. Every input word and partial tail word must affect the accumulator through a carry-less product with a derived key; do not ignore odd words, do not just xor the tail word into both low and high limbs, and do not use a final reduction that makes `(x, x)` or all short inputs fold to zero. Length mixing and final-key mixing must be asymmetric and observable: do not create a length hash as `(v, v)` immediately followed by `lo ^ hi`, do not reduce only as `lo ^ hi` after adding identical values to both halves, and do not read polynomial/final/key-length words unless the return value actually depends on them. For same-length inputs, if semantic checks compare `hash(x) ^ hash(x with one bit flipped)` across different base values, the accumulator-to-output fold must be GF(2)-linear in the message accumulator: use XOR, fixed shifts, rotates, and xors with final/length keys; do not use integer `wrapping_mul`, `wrapping_add`, or arithmetic carries on accumulator-derived values in that short-input fold. Keep reductions in the hash hot path bounded: use fixed limb folds, fixed small rounds, or a direct 128-to-64 fold; do not loop while a high product half remains nonzero or clear one high bit at a time for every message block. Keep input mixing over GF(2): byte/word contributions should combine with XOR and carry-less products, so flipping the same input bit under the same key produces the same xor delta regardless of the original byte value for the same length; if that xor delta depends on the original byte value, an integer multiply/add path probably leaked in. The top-level hash path and hasher methods must not start with length asserts for internal table sizes. Use scalar code unless all target features and imports for intrinsics already exist.

rules.title: Use wrapping arithmetic for unsigned PRNG key expansion
rules.trigger: C unsigned PRNG, xorshift, seed expansion, or random-key generation updates state with shifts, xors, and addition.
rules.goal: Preserve C unsigned overflow behavior while generating the same deterministic key or random byte sequence shape.
rules.constraint: Do not use normal Rust +, *, or shift expressions when C unsigned arithmetic can wrap in debug builds.
rules.risk: The generated key helper can compile but panic at runtime on overflow before hash or sequence tests observe semantics.
rules.guidance: For xorshift-style state updates and random key expansion, use wrapping_add, wrapping_mul, wrapping_shl, and wrapping_shr where C uses unsigned arithmetic. Advance state exactly once per generated word and serialize words with the byte order used by the C helper or Rust interface contract.

rules.title: Keep bit buffers byte-safe and decoder-owned
rules.trigger: A bit writer/reader or floating-point delta codec fails with shift overflow, wrong decoded values, or a raw bit reader consuming the stream without updating decoder state.
rules.goal: Preserve bit-exact packing while avoiding Rust shift panics and keeping decoded value, leading-zero, trailing-zero, and termination state in the decoder.
rules.constraint: Do not shift a u8 by 8, a u32 by 32, a u64 by 64, or any integer by its bit width in Rust. Do not write delta payload bits after emitting the unchanged-value marker for a zero xor delta. Do not leave reachable bit reader setup or read-next entrypoints as `unimplemented!()`, `todo!()`, or `panic!("not implemented")`. Do not implement a decoder-state function on the raw bit-reader receiver just because a generated interface placed a similarly named stub there; use the receiver that owns previous value, leading/trailing counts, finished flag, and error state. Do not repair only the first shift panic if the same bitstream also has a decoder state machine in the candidate context.
rules.risk: The encoder can produce plausible bytes but panic at byte-aligned writes; after that panic is fixed, the decoder can still return one correct first value followed by zeros or huge repeated values if the marker-bit polarity, field widths, significant-bit count, refill ordering, or previous-value xor update is wrong. A stored significant-length field of zero can also be misread as zero payload bits instead of a full-width payload.
rules.guidance: For byte-aligned writes, widen the byte before shifting, for example `((b as u16) << bit_count) as u8`, and handle `bit_count == 8` and `nbits == 64` as explicit cases so no runtime shift equals the type width. In a multi-bit writer, also handle `nbits == 0`, `nbits == word_bits`, and `remaining == word_bits` before evaluating expressions like `u << (64 - nbits)`, `1 << nbits`, `word << used`, or `value >> (word_bits - take)`, because any of those can become a shift by the full type width in debug builds. Mask construction should branch: all bits set for a full-width count, zero for a zero count, otherwise `(1u64 << nbits) - 1` on a wide enough type. For delta-coded floating streams, repair the writer and decoder together when both are listed. In the encoder, after computing `delta = current_bits ^ previous_bits`, the zero-delta branch must write exactly the unchanged marker bit and then update/return without computing leading/trailing zeros or writing a second control bit, significant-bit count, or payload; continuing into the changed-value payload path after a zero marker misaligns every later decode. For bit readers, keep `n`, `v`, and the remaining slice consistent after every reset, read, and refill. A reset/setup method must bind the provided byte slice, set `len`, clear `n` and `v`, then call the refill helper; it must not be a stub just because a higher-level decoder also calls `read_bits`. When a read crosses a refill boundary, combine the old high bits and new high bits in the same order as the writer emitted them, not by reusing the old bit count as a right-shift amount without checking alignment. The block decoder should execute the decoder's own `read_next` semantics on the struct that owns `val`, `leading`, `trailing`, `finished`, and `err`; if only an unrelated raw bit-reader `read_next` stub is listed, inline the decoder-state machine in the block decoder rather than filling the raw reader with fields it does not have. If a raw bit-reader `read_next` callable is still reachable by tests, implement it as a simple bit-availability/read-bit operation or delegate to `read_bit`, but do not leave it as a panic. The decoder state machine must handle the first raw value without consuming another marker bit, then read the changed-value bit. If that bit is 1, read the second control bit with the same polarity as the writer: second bit 1 means a new leading count plus significant-bit count follows, while second bit 0 means reuse the previous leading/trailing window. For this common layout, leading count is a 5-bit field and significant count is a 6-bit field; treat a stored significant count of zero as 64 bits when that is the C convention, reject or flag impossible `leading + significant_bits > 64` instead of underflowing, compute `trailing = 64 - leading - significant_bits`, xor `(payload << trailing)` into the previous value, and stop only on the stream sentinel or a true read error. If a trial patch fixes a shift panic but then decodes one correct first value followed by zeros or huge repeated values, keep the shift fix and additionally fix this encoder zero-delta/control-bit and decoder state/refill logic in the same patch rather than rolling the writer fix back.
